mistakes.close: Looking for a (close). It is called (dismiss): close is a native member of window and of , and no public member of the system is named after something native.
mistakes.icon: Passing it an icon. You cannot, and that is on purpose: the caller chooses the severity, the system supplies the drawing. That way nobody ends up with a triangle on a success message.
mistakes.infoBlue: Using variant="info" and expecting blue. Info is neutral. Blue means “this is clickable”.
mistakes.selfClosing: Expecting it to close by itself when close is pressed. It does not close: it emits. Whoever put it there decides, because “the user closed it” and “the condition has ended” are different facts.

banner.notApplicable: One: sizes, because the banner has only one. It is written above rather than deleted.

props.caption: Properties of <ewms-banner>
props.description: Optional second line. A one-line banner is a legitimate banner.
props.dismiss: Emitted when close is pressed. It is NOT called (close): close is native on window and on . The banner does not take itself off the screen.
props.dismissLabel: Accessible name of the close button. It has a default instead of being required: a banner without a button should not pay that tax.
props.dismissible: Shows the close button. Without it there is no button, and no way to close the banner.
props.severityLabel: Required. The severity in words, for the icon's accessible name. Required in the type: it is the only cue that does not depend on seeing the colour.
props.title: Required. The headline, already translated by the consumer. The design system speaks no language.
props.variant: The severity. It chooses the icon, the colour family and the role. Info is called Info and painted neutral: there is no info family.

purpose.decide: If a decision is needed before carrying on, use a Dialog. A banner does not block, and a destructive action needs friction.
purpose.fieldError: If the error belongs to a field, use the Input's hint. A banner above a form forces people to hunt for which of the twelve fields failed.
purpose.icon: Four semantic variants. The component chooses the icon from the variant; the consumer does not pass it.
purpose.justHappened: If the message is something that has just happened, use a Toast. “Saved” is not a condition: it is a fact that is fully told in three seconds.
purpose.solves: A message that lives in the layout and stays until someone closes it. It pushes the content down, it is not an overlay, and that is why it suits a condition that is still true: this warehouse is under a cycle count, this shipment has an issue.

sizes.fits: There is no size. A banner takes the width of its container and grows with its content; the only height variable is whether it has a description or not, and that is in the matrix above.

icon.measured: Measured on the rendered SVG in the variants section, not written here. The icon does not grow with the severity: a Danger with a bigger icon than an Info is exactly the “fix” someone adds six months later.

doubleSubmit.focus: While it loads, the button keeps the focus: it is disabled with aria-disabled and not with the native attribute, because the native one takes it out of the tab order just after it has received Enter, and the focus would drop to the .
doubleSubmit.intro: A click goes into Loading and comes back on its own. While it loads, the content is hidden with visibility and not with display, so the box does not change size and nothing next to it moves. The counter is the proof: however many times you press it while it spins, it goes up only once.

iconOnly.intro: With [iconOnly]="true" the button loses its text and gains two rules: the box is square —the control height also used as the width— and label is required: it is the accessible name and the tooltip, which is added automatically. Without label, development mode throws an error.
iconOnly.rowFrame: The real case: a table row
iconOnly.title: Icon only
iconOnly.toggles: A toggle (the favourites star) passes pressed; a menu or panel trigger, expanded and controls. They are inputs and not attributes: on they would land on an element with no role.

button.notApplicable: None: all eight apply to this component. The section is written out all the same, because other sheets will have gaps, and a visible gap is information.

props.caption: Properties of <ewms-button>
props.content: Projected text. The button's text. It arrives already translated by the consumer: the system speaks no language.
props.controls: aria-controls: the id of the panel or menu it opens.
props.disabled: Independent of loading. Uses the native disabled attribute.
props.icon: A name from the closed catalogue. A name outside the list does not compile. It is rendered without a label: it is decorative, the button's text already says it.
props.iconOnly: No visible text: a square box, and label becomes the name and the tooltip.
props.iconPosition: Only applies if there is an icon.
props.label: Required with iconOnly (an error in development mode). It arrives translated.
props.loading: Hides the content without changing the size, sets aria-busy and aria-disabled, and ignores the click. It does not use the native disabled, so as not to lose the focus.
props.pressedExpanded: aria-pressed and aria-expanded. null leaves them out: it is not a toggle.
props.size: The three control heights, shared with Input and Select.
props.type:
With submit, inside a
, Enter in any field submits it. The default changes nothing that already existed: a button only submits if someone wrote it that way on purpose.
props.variant: The emphasis. A single Primary per view or form. Link is text with no box, in sm and md, for actions inside a notice or a line.

purpose.doubleSubmit: It also brings the double-submit guard, which is why an operator does not create two receipts by double-clicking.
purpose.frame: With text and icon only: the same component
purpose.iconOnlyNote: Icon only uses its label as the name and as the tooltip: give it focus with Tab and it appears. The second one is in Loading and measures exactly the same as the first.
purpose.navigates: If it navigates, it is a link. A button that leads to another URL breaks opening in a new tab, copying the link and the “back” button. If the result is an address, use an .
purpose.onePrimary: If there is more than one Primary in the view, none of them is the main one. The others are Secondary.
purpose.solves: Triggers an action on the current screen: save, confirm, filter, delete. The emphasis comes from the variant, not from the size or a hand-picked colour.
purpose.textFirst: If there is room for text, use text. Icon only (iconOnly) is for when the word does not fit —rows, dense bars—, not for when it looks tidier.

sizes.measured: The heights above are measured on the rendered button, not written into the page: the block exists to prove 32/40/48, and a transcribed number proves nothing. The icon drops to sm in Small and stays at md in Medium and Large, so that it does not unbalance a toolbar.

states.caption: Five variants by five states
states.intro: Truly rendered, not screenshots. Disabled and Loading are real inputs of the component. Hover and Focus cannot be held still, so each cell gets the same token its own rule would apply.

submit.defaultType: type is 'button' by default, and that does not change: a button only submits if someone wrote it that way on purpose. What was closed in DS-5 is the cost that rule had, which showed up while building the DS-4 example screen — a multi-field form with no submit button does not submit with Enter either, because the browser's implicit submission needs a submit button to exist. Saving was a click or Ctrl+S, and Enter inside a field, which is what everybody does, did nothing.
submit.onePath: With type="submit" there is a single path and three ways into it: Enter in any field, the button, and the shortcut — which calls requestSubmit() and not click(), because pressing a button is one way of submitting, not the submission itself. All three raise a submit, so whatever is added to submitting tomorrow —a validation, a guard, a confirmation— applies to all three. The double-submit guard does not change: loading blocks the second one.
submit.title: Submitting a form (DS-5)

variants.canonical: The names are canonical: Danger, never “Destructive” or “Delete”. And there is no “custom” variant — a component with that name ends up as the dumping ground for everything that did not fit anywhere else.
variants.ghostHover: Ghost darkens its text on hover: it goes from --color-bg-primary to --color-bg-primary-hover, the same gesture with which Primary darkens its background. It is not an exception: the brand blue on --color-ghost-hover measures 4.38:1 and 1.4.3 asks for 4.5:1; the hover shade measures 5.65:1.
variants.link: Link is a button that looks like text: no background or border, in Small and Medium, for an action inside a notice or a line —retry, clear the filters, go to the field with the error—. It does something; if it led to another address, it would be an . It rests on --color-bg-primary-hover and is underlined on hover: the brand blue measures 4.31:1 on --color-danger-surface, where the Select's retry lives, and the hover shade 5.54:1.

accent.bar: Brand Foundations pairs that tint with a 3 px accent bar because the tint on its own sits a hair away from --color-ghost-hover, and a WMS puts ghost buttons inside selectable rows. The card does not need the bar: its whole outline turns action blue, which is the same guarantee drawn larger. The check in the corner is the third cue.
accent.signals: Three signals for a single state, and none of the three is colour alone: that is exactly what WCAG 1.4.1 asks for.
accent.title: --color-row-selected never goes alone, and here the accent is the whole border

contract.outputs: One, and model() declares it: (valueChange). The value travels through [formField] inside a form and through [(value)] outside one. As in the Select, and for the same reason: there is no native here whose change has to be stopped.

demo.keyboard: Try it with the keyboard. A single Tab enters the group, and it lands on the chosen card. The arrows move and choose —selection follows focus, which is what a native radio group does—, skip the disabled one and wrap around at the ends. Space chooses the focused one. Enter does nothing here on purpose: it belongs to the surrounding form, which is what makes a keyboard-driven form fast.

finding.caption: The neighbours, measured, on --color-row-selected
finding.measure: --color-text-secondary on --color-row-selected measures 4.35:1 and falls short of the 4.5:1 that WCAG 1.4.3 requires for normal text. axe found it on this very page: the chosen card's meta line was text-caption text-secondary, which is the natural thing to write.
finding.noToken: No token was touched and no test was weakened. There is no intermediate primitive between navy-46 and navy-28, so the way out is not “darken the secondary a little”: that would be a new colour primitive, which is a design decision and gets reported. Meanwhile the demo above uses the card's foreground colour, and the finding stays written here.
finding.scope: It is a combination the specification allows and that had never been drawn —the same failure mode the hovered Ghost found in DS-2—, and it is not exclusive to the card: it affects the Table, whose selected rows carry caption and mono text.

keyboard.caption: The keyboard contract, implemented in the card and coordinated by the group
keyboard.enter: Nothing, on purpose. In a radio group Enter belongs to the form: it submits. Swallowing it here would break the gesture that makes a keyboard form fast.
keyboard.followsFocus: Selection follows focus, and it is not an invention: in a radio group the arrows change the answer, they do not browse it. Browsing without choosing is the listbox pattern, and this is not one. That is also why it wraps around, unlike the Select panel: a panel is a list being walked, and reaching its end is information; a group of four cards is a closed set, and stopping at the last one only means pressing the other arrow.
keyboard.next: Moves to and chooses the next eligible card. Wraps around at the end.
keyboard.space: Chooses the focused card. It also stops the scroll, which is the last thing someone choosing wants.
keyboard.tab: Enters the group only once, on the chosen card — or on the first eligible one if none is chosen. A group with nothing chosen is still reachable, which is how it always starts.
keyboard.title: Accessibility: the keyboard of a radio group

mistakes.bindCard: Binding the form to the card. It binds to the group. The card carries optionValue precisely so that two members called value in the same tree are not confused.
mistakes.buttonInside: Putting a button inside a selectable card. It is a control inside another control: one of the two takes the click and the keyboard becomes ambiguous. Buttons go in the footer of a content card.
mistakes.disabledTrue: Putting [disabled]="true" on the group and expecting form.enable() to bring it back. It does not: whoever disables wins, and nobody re-enables. A form-driven control simply does not pass that input.
mistakes.standaloneClick: Expecting a standalone card to react to a click. Outside a group it is not a control: it has no role, no focus and holds nothing.

cards.notApplicable: One: sizes, because the card has no scale. It is written above rather than deleted.

props.body: The body. It is the default slot, so a selectable card is written with its content directly inside.
props.caption: Properties of <ewms-card> and <ewms-card-group>
props.cardDisabled: The card's own disabled. The group's is added with OR, never subtracted.
props.footer: Footer slot, for the primary actions of a content card.
props.groupDisabled: Added with OR to each card's own. Disables every card and empties the tab stop. Inside a form it is set by the schema's disabled() rule.
props.header: Header slot. An attribute on any element, not a directive.
props.label: Required. Names the radiogroup for assistive technology. Already translated.
props.optionValue: What this card is worth when it is the chosen one. Meaningless outside a group. It is not called value: value belongs to the group, which is what the form binds to.
props.value: The chosen value. It seeds the control; after that writeValue rules, that is, the form.

purpose.multiple: If several have to be chosen, it does not exist yet. The group is single-select by design; multi-select is declared as pending in the sheet.
purpose.navigates: If the whole card navigates somewhere else, use a link. This is a form control: its job is to hold a value, not to take you to a route.
purpose.shortText: If the options are short text, use Radio. A card exists to show context —a meta line, an icon, a number—; without any of that it is a radio with an expensive border around it.
purpose.solves: Two uses under one name, as the sheet says. Inside an it is an option: choosing with more visual context than a radio. Anywhere else it is a container: header, body and footer, with no state of its own.
purpose.which: Which of the two it is comes from where it is written, not from a property. See block 4.

sizes.body: There is no size. A card is sized by its content and by the width the layout leaves it, not by the 32 / 40 / 48 control scale: it does not line up with a button in a row, which is the only reason that scale exists.
sizes.fixed: The only fixed things are the inner padding and the radius, and both come from tokens — they are in the next block.
sizes.title: Does not apply — the card has no scale

states.caption: The card's two uses by its four states
states.contentSame: The content card is the same in all four columns, and that is the information. It has no hover, no selection and cannot be disabled: it is layout. The row above is the one that changes.
states.forced: Hover is the only forced cell, with the same token the component's rule uses (--color-border-strong): nobody can hold the pointer still over a grid. Focus is missing, for the same reason as in the Input and the Select: the ring is a :focus-visible box-shadow, and a wrapping class cannot produce it without lying about when it appears. Walk through it with Tab in the demo above, which is where it truly shows.

a11y.domProperty: indeterminate only exists as a DOM property. There is no HTML attribute: writing indeterminate="true" in a template sets an unknown attribute, the box renders unchecked, and nothing anywhere reports a problem. It has to be assigned to the element — here with an effect, because the input changes during the component's lifetime.
a11y.glyph: The glyph is an overlaid sibling with pointer-events-none, not a child: an cannot have children, and this way no pixel of the box has two things fighting over it.
a11y.mixed: aria-checked carries mixed when indeterminate, not a boolean: the visual difference between checked and indeterminate is a glyph inside an otherwise identical box.
a11y.noAriaDisabled: There is no aria-disabled next to the native disabled: the native attribute already carries the state, and the two together would announce it twice.

anatomy.caption: Tokens that <ewms-checkbox> consumes
anatomy.intro: The same list as the Radio's, because they share it in the code: a box, a border, a glyph and a row that is the clickable area, written only once. Only the corner radius and the glyph are written twice.
anatomy.radius: The only thing of its own: the checkbox's corner radius is rounded-sm (4 px). The Radio uses rounded-full.

contract.foundBy: It was caught by a test that failed with a raw Event instead of the boolean, not by a review. The sheet asked for (change); it has since been corrected.
contract.inputs: The five in the table in block 3. None is required by the type, but one of label or ariaLabel is required in practice.
contract.outputs: (checkedChange), and the name is structural. change is a native event, and it bubbles: an output with that name puts two different things in a single binding —this component's boolean and the raw Event rising from the inner — and the handler runs twice with two types of argument. ESLint's no-output-native rule forbids it for exactly that reason.
contract.stopPropagation: And there is a second half: the component calls stopPropagation() on the native change. That is not tidiness. This component publishes checkedChange; the inner is an implementation detail. Letting its event out would give the consumer a second, undocumented event whose target is that private element — something to bind to, to read the flag from, and that the next internal change breaks.

demo.frame: Checklist with “select all”
demo.intro: The case that justifies the third state: a “select all” checkbox over a list where some rows are ticked and others are not.
demo.keepsIndeterminate: When a box is clicked, the component does not clear indeterminate on its own: it is the consumer's statement about a set of other things, and only the consumer knows whether this click settled it. Guessing would make the “select all” box flicker out of the mixed state on a click that did not select everything.
demo.wholeRow: The whole row is the clickable area —box, gap and text— because the wraps the control instead of pointing at it with for/id. There is no pair of identifiers to keep in sync, and the text is not decoration next to the control: it is part of the control.

disabledRule.gain: The gain is the one the old OR rule was after, by another route: whoever writes [disabled]="true" cannot be re-enabled by the form, because the form does not touch that field.
disabledRule.noMix: They are not combined because Angular does not allow it: binding [disabled] on the same node as [formField] is a compile error (NG8022). The field has one owner, and so two sources are never left disagreeing.
disabledRule.oneOwner: One owner at a time. Outside a form, the disabled input. Inside one, the schema's disabled(path.x, …) rule.
disabledRule.same: It holds exactly the same for the Radio, the Toggle, the Input and the Select.
disabledRule.title: The disabled rule — the most surprising one

mistakes.change: Listening to (change). It does not exist as an output, and the native one is stopped inside. It is (checkedChange).
mistakes.indeterminate: Expecting indeterminate to switch itself off on click. It does not: the statement belongs to the consumer.
mistakes.instant: Using it for something that applies instantly. That is the Toggle.
mistakes.noName: Leaving it without label or ariaLabel. It compiles, and it has no accessible name.

checkbox.notApplicable: One: variants. It is written above rather than deleted.

props.ariaLabel: The accessible name when there is no visible text: a column of checkboxes, one per row, where the name has to say WHICH row.
props.caption: <ewms-checkbox> properties
props.checked: Seeds the state. After that the form is in charge: the base class takes it as the seed of a linkedSignal, and writeValue overrides it.
props.checkedChange: It is NOT called (change): that name is native and it bubbles. See block 8. It is also the name the Toggle already had, so both selection controls read the same.
props.disabled: Outside a form. Inside one, the schema's disabled() rule sets it — see block 8.
props.indeterminate: Neither checked nor unchecked: the “select all” box when some rows are chosen. It wins over checked, both visually and in what is announced.
props.label: Visible text next to the box, already translated. Optional because it is not always labelled in place — the header of a selectable table is the case in point.

purpose.native: It is a native with appearance-none, not a painted : that way the role, the space bar, the tab order, the ring on the element that really has the focus and the name given by the that wraps it all come for free.
purpose.notRadio: If the options exclude each other, it is a Radio.
purpose.notTerms: If it is a single required option —accepting some terms— check whether it ought to be a step in the flow rather than a checkbox.
purpose.notToggle: If it applies the moment you touch it, it is a Toggle. It is the most common confusion in this library, and it is not about how they look: the Toggle acts there and then, the Checkbox marks something that is confirmed later. Getting it wrong leaves a Save button next to a setting that has already been applied, or silently discards a selection someone believed they had made.
purpose.solves: A selection inside a form, confirmed later by something else: a Save button, a bulk action, a submission. An 18×18 box with a tick, a dash or nothing inside.

sizes.mismatch: The token declares a border of one and a half and the browser paints one: Chromium rounds a sub-pixel border down, at any screen density. What the component owes is the token; what the browser does with it is the browser's business — which is why the E2E asserts the declaration and not the used value, or it would be asserting someone else's rounding rule.
sizes.mismatchTitle: The last two numbers do not match, and it is right that this shows
sizes.single: 18×18 px, full stop. It does not use the 32 / 40 / 48 scale of the Button, the Input and the Select, on purpose: a checkbox is not sized to line up with a button, it is sized to sit next to a line of text.
sizes.title: Just one — and it is not the control scale

states.caption: Three values by four states
states.disabledFirst: Disabled goes first and has no hover: a control that cannot be operated should not light up under the pointer.
states.hoverColumn: The Hover column only changes something in the first row, and that is correct: hover paints the border blue, and in “Checked” and “Indeterminate” the border is already blue. The cell is not broken; the state has nothing to add there.
states.intro: The three values against the four states. Disabled is a real input; Hover and Focus cannot be held still, so each cell gets the same token its own rule would apply.
states.sameBox: Checked and indeterminate look almost the same: same blue box, different glyph. It is what the sheet asks for, and that is exactly why the state cannot be read from the colour — and why aria-checked carries mixed and not a boolean. Someone who is not looking at the screen gets the state from there and nowhere else.

variants.ariaLabelNote: The second one has no visible text: its name comes from ariaLabel, which exists because the Table needs one checkbox per row and a “select all” in the header, none of them with text beside it. One of the two is required in practice: with neither, the control has no accessible name and axe fails. The type cannot say “exactly one of these two”, so the spec asserts it.
variants.none: There is no variant: there is no such thing as “the primary checkbox”. What there is, is three values —unchecked, checked and indeterminate— and that is the axis of the matrix.

brandBlue.body: It is in tokens.css with no utility in the Tailwind theme, with its reason written next to it: its only planned use (the Dashboard KPI icons) clashes with the rule above, and the decision is deferred until those KPIs are built. Do not delete it because it looks dead.
brandBlue.primary: The action value the components do consume is --color-bg-primary, which today points to the same primitive. Two different names because they mean different things.
brandBlue.title: --color-brand-blue has no utility, and that is on purpose

contrast.caption: Pairs checked ({{ count }})
contrast.intro: No number in this table is transcribed. The page reads the two tokens, converts them to channels and works out the WCAG ratio in the browser. If someone moves a token and breaks a contrast, the table gives it away on its own — which is the whole point of calculating it instead of writing it down.
contrast.minimums: Minimums: {{ text }}:1 for text (1.4.3) and {{ nonText }}:1 for borders and components (1.4.11). Exempt is not a softer “fail”: a disabled control is exempt under the standard, and a decorative divider is not a control.

notes.activeOption: The active option in the Select panel has this background.
notes.caption: Caption and metadata on a surface: it is 12 px text.
notes.controlBorder: A border that defines a control (WCAG 1.4.11).
notes.controlBorderHoverWorst: The worst case for the border hover.
notes.controlBorderOnCanvas: The same border on the canvas.
notes.dangerButton: Text on the Danger button. It is the case that forced this token to be white rather than text-on-dark.
notes.disabledDanger: The same calculation for disabled Danger.
notes.disabledOnSecondary: Disabled text on a secondary surface.
notes.disabledPrimary: Disabled control: exempt from 1.4.3. Noted as pending with product in the Button sheet.
notes.divider: Decorative divider: exempt. Never the border of a control.
notes.familyText: The family's text on its own surface.
notes.focusRing: The ring contrasts with the surface, not with the control: that is why it has a gap.
notes.focusRingOnDark: It exists because the brand blue on navy has no room to breathe.
notes.neutralBadge: Neutral badge: surface + text, never solid + white.
notes.primaryOnSurface: Primary text on the white surface.
notes.secondaryOnSecondary: Secondary text on a secondary surface.
notes.secondaryWorst: The worst case for secondary text.
notes.toggleThumb: The thumb of a Toggle that is on and disabled, against its track.

contrast.title: Contrast, worked out here

header.layers: Two layers. At the bottom, the primitives: the raw values, named for what they are. On top, the semantic tokens: named for their role, each aliasing a primitive. No component touches the bottom layer — rebranding means changing which primitive a semantic token points to, without touching a single component.
header.live: Everything shown here is read live from tokens.css. The primitives are not even written on this page: they are discovered by walking the stylesheet, so a new shade shows up on its own.

primitives.intro: The shade is the value's CIE L* lightness, rounded: 0 is black, 100 is white. It is not an invented scale; it comes from the value, which is why the contrast can be read at a glance.
primitives.title: Layer 1 — primitives

translucent.note: Shadows and overlay. Navy and not black: a shadow tinted with the brand colour blends in, a grey one looks dirty. They sit on a chequerboard so that the transparency shows.
translucent.title: translucent navy

blue.body: The brand blue is reserved exclusively for action. Nothing informational, decorative or status-related uses blue. It is a strong rule, cheap to keep up, and it makes the interface readable without having to think about it.
blue.frame: Action and non-action, side by side
blue.title: Blue means “this is clickable”

noInfo.badge: For the same reason Badge/Neutral is built with surface + text and not with solid + white: the solid only reaches 4.19:1, below AA. It is also the natural choice for a “stateless” badge.
noInfo.body: Informational content uses neutral. The natural informational blue sat at 1.76:1 from the action blue: indistinguishable in practice. With neutral they never compete.
noInfo.title: There is no info family

semantic.intro: Each row shows which primitive it points to. That arrow is the whole concept.

anatomy.intl: Month and day names, the day/month/year order and the first day of the week come from Intl with the active locale: nothing is written by hand. If the browser does not know the first day of the week, it is Monday.

contract.keysCalendar: In the calendar: <kbd>← →</kbd> one day, <kbd>↑ ↓</kbd> one week, <kbd>Page Up</kbd> / <kbd>Page Down</kbd> one month (with <kbd>Shift</kbd>, one year), <kbd>Home</kbd> / <kbd>End</kbd> the week, <kbd>Enter</kbd> picks.
contract.keysDialog: <kbd>Esc</kbd> closes without picking and returns the focus to the button; <kbd>Tab</kbd> does not leave the dialog. In the field, <kbd>Alt</kbd>+<kbd>↓</kbd> opens it.
contract.messages: The texts (choose date, previous month, next month) and the locale are provided once with EWMS_DATE_PICKER_MESSAGES. The locale is a getter in the shell because the app changes language without reloading; without it, LOCALE_ID is used.

props.caption: <ewms-date-picker> properties
props.label: Required. Visible, linked by for/id.
props.limits: 'YYYY-MM-DD'. Days outside it are shown and can be walked through, but not picked.
props.mode: A 'YYYY-MM-DD' date, or the table’s DateRange '{ from, to }'.
props.texts: As in the Input. The hint goes through aria-describedby.

purpose.knownDate: For a date known by heart (a date of birth, the expiry of a printed lot): typing it is quicker than going through the years; the field accepts it all the same.
purpose.native: Our own, not : the native one shows the operating system’s format even when the app is in another language, and it takes no tokens.
purpose.noTime: For a time of day: it has none.
purpose.solves: A date, or a period, in the app’s language: it is typed the way it reads here (3/16/2026) or picked from a calendar you can walk through entirely with the keyboard. The value is 'YYYY-MM-DD', with no time zone.

sizes.intro: The Input’s three (32 / 40 / 48) for the field. The calendar has just one: 32 px days, above the WCAG 2.5.8 minimum of 24.

states.days: The field is the Input’s box: default, focus, error and disabled are the ones in its matrix. In the calendar, a day can be today (ring), selected (action background), out of range (grey, it can be walked through but not picked) and active (focus ring). You can see them for real by opening the demo.

variants.intro: mode="range": two picks in the calendar, in any order, build the DateRange the Table filter already uses. Typed, it takes a dash between the two dates.

closed.body: Only the {{ total }} icons below exist, and a name outside the list does not compile. Adding one means editing icons.manifest.json and running npm run icons:build, in a PR. An is never pasted into a template: CI gate 11 blocks it.
closed.title: The catalogue is closed

sizes.intro: The stroke gets thinner as the icon grows, so that the visible weight stays even next to the text. Values read live from tokens.css.
sizes.title: Sizes and stroke compensation

a11y.hint: The hint is a description, connected with aria-describedby, and never part of the name: a field called “SKU Format ABC-123” is a field nobody can ask for by name.
a11y.label: A real , always rendered. The required asterisk is aria-hidden: the native attribute already makes the screen reader say “required”, and the glyph would say it twice — and as the word “asterisk”.
a11y.readOnly: readOnly is written as a DOM property, not as an attribute: the attribute is presence-or-absence, so binding false to it would still leave the field read-only. It is also why read-only is not built with disabled: a read-only field keeps the focus, its tab stop and text selection, and a disabled one loses all three.

anatomy.caption: Tokens that <ewms-input> consumes
anatomy.intro: Which token controls each part, read live. The heights and the type scale are not redefined for the field: they are the Button’s, imported. There is a single copy of the control scale in the whole system.

contract.gate10: There is a second, smaller reason: gate 10 reads every string literal in a .ts as a possible class name, and one of the two native names is also a default Tailwind utility, so binding it from an inline template broke the build.
contract.inputs: The ones in the table in block 3. label is the only one the type requires. disabled and the other inputs of the contract are filled in by [formField] — see below.
contract.outputs: (fieldFocus) and (fieldBlur), and the prefix is structural. An output named like the native event clashes with it: the inner emits focus and blur, which bubble up and land in the same consumer binding, which then receives a FocusEvent instead of the component’s void. ESLint’s no-output-native rule flags it on its own.
contract.suffixAbsent: If they are not passed, the button is not rendered: absent is better than present and nameless. It is also why this page writes them out in plain sight, in the active language — so that the showroom is not the only place where they are read.
contract.suffixLabels: showPasswordLabel, hidePasswordLabel and clearLabel exist because the suffix is an , which requires a translated accessible name, and the design system speaks no language to make one up. The alternatives were a nameless button —it fails axe and is unusable by voice— or a required input on every text field that will never hold a password.
contract.suffixTitle: The three texts of the suffix buttons
contract.vaultSheet: The vault sheet asked for (focus) and (blur): they were written before the clash was known, and the sheet has since been corrected. It is the same family of mistake as the Tooltip’s disabled — a member of the public API is not named after something the native element already emits or exposes.

demo.frame: A real form, with its value live
demo.intro: Inside a real signal form. The component is a FormValueControl: what has to be shown is that [formField] reaches it, that typing updates the field and that leaving the field marks it as touched. A standalone input proves none of the three.

password.hint: The eye button only appears because it was given both its texts.
password.label: Operator password

search.hint: The × only appears once there is something to clear.
search.label: Search location

sku.hint: Format ABC-00000-X. Focus me with Tab to see the ring.
sku.label: Item SKU

demo.touch: The value above comes from the field in form(), not from a local copy: if the component stopped writing to it, that line would stay still while the box fills up with letters. (touch) is emitted only on blur, never when the value changes: a field someone is still typing in is not yet “touched”, and marking it earlier would make the validation messages appear mid-keystroke.

mistakes.disabled: Setting [disabled]="true" and then calling form.enable(). It is not re-enabled: isDisabled = disabled() || disabledByForm(). Whoever disables wins, and nobody re-enables. For the form to handle it, do not pass the input.
mistakes.nativeEvents: Listening to (focus) or (blur). You get the native event, not the component’s. They are (fieldFocus) and (fieldBlur).
mistakes.placeholder: Using the placeholder as the name. It disappears at the first character, and several screen readers never announce it.
mistakes.stateError: Expecting state="error" to validate. It does not. It is the form that decides, and it says so through that input.

input.notApplicable: None. The matrix has a declared gap —Focus— and it is explained in its block instead of being disguised.

props.caption: <ewms-input> properties
props.clearLabel: Accessible name of the × that empties a search field. Without it the button is not rendered.
props.disabled: Inside a form it is set by the schema’s disabled() rule: Angular forbids binding [disabled] on the same node as [formField].
props.fieldBlur: The same for (blur). It is also where the form receives onTouched.
props.fieldFocus: Prefixed on purpose: the native (focus) bubbles up to the same consumer binding. See block 8.
props.hint: Help below the field, connected with aria-describedby. It turns danger-coloured when state="error".
props.label: Required. Rendered as a real . A placeholder is not a name: it disappears at the first character and several screen readers never announce it.
props.placeholder: Sample text inside the field. It never replaces the label.
props.required: Paints the asterisk next to the label and sets the native attribute.
props.showPasswordLabel: Accessible name of the show-password button, already translated. Without it (and without hidePasswordLabel) the button is NOT rendered.
props.size: The same three control heights as the Button and the Select: 32 / 40 / 48.
props.state: Purely visual: the component validates nothing. Whoever decides whether a value is wrong is the parent form.

purpose.closedList: If the option comes from a closed list, it is a Select. An input with a made-up autocomplete on top is not this component.
purpose.nativeControl: The border and the ring sit on the native control, not on a wrapper: the prefix icon and the suffix button are overlaid on top of it, and the text is kept clear with padding. Wrapping it in a bordered box would move the ring to something that does not have the focus.
purpose.noValidation: It validates nothing. state="error" is a snapshot. Whoever decides whether a value is wrong is the parent form — and that is what keeps the component out of each project’s validation conventions.
purpose.placeholder: The placeholder is not the label. If you are about to use only a placeholder, what is missing is the label — and here it is required, so it does not compile.
purpose.solves: A single-line or multi-line text field. It shares its box with —same heights, same type scale, same radius, same border colours and same focus ring— so a form row with an input, a select and a button lines up without anyone measuring.

sizes.intro: Three, and they are the same as the Button’s. It is not a coincidence that gets documented: it is a rule, and the two heights below are measured and compared to prove it.
sizes.padding: The horizontal padding does differ —10 / 12 / 14 in the field against 12 / 16 / 20 in the button— and also on purpose: the button’s keeps its text away from the border, the field’s keeps the cursor away from the border, and a field is usually much wider than its content. Copying the button’s would push the text of every field a third of a centimetre further in than the design asks for.

states.caption: Four states by three sizes, all with real inputs

errorWins.body: A field in error that receives the focus keeps the danger border and gets the normal focus ring on top. The system has exactly one focus colour, everywhere; a second colour would make the ring mean two different things.
errorWins.title: Error wins over Focus

states.intro: The four states against the three sizes. All twelve are real inputs: no cell is painted with a class, so what you see is the component and not an imitation.
states.noFocus: Focus is missing, and on purpose. The border colour is applied as an inline style, tied to the component’s own focus signal; a wrapping class cannot beat it, so a forced “Focus” cell would show the ring with the wrong border. That is just lying more neatly. The real focus is above, in the field you reach with Tab.

readOnly.body: Read-only text is real content that someone may need to read and copy: it keeps the primary colour and the normal cursor, and only the grey background says “this cannot be edited here”. Painting it with text-disabled would make an unchangeable value look like an unavailable one, and to whoever reads the screen those two mean opposite things.
readOnly.title: Disabled and Read-only share the background and nothing else

variants.icons: Decorative icons —the magnifying glass in search— are at sm (16 px) in all three sizes, with no label: the field already has a name from its . The eye and the × are something else: they are pressed, so they are , and there the accessible name is mandatory.
variants.intro: Five types. They are not style variants —the system has no “secondary input”— but variants of what is typed inside, and each one changes something real: the alignment, an icon, a button, or the whole element.

notes.number: Right-aligned: numbers are compared digit by digit.
notes.password: Show/hide suffix button. It only appears with its two texts.
notes.search: Prefix icon, and a clear button when there is something to clear.
notes.textarea: A different element, same border and same radius. No manual resizing.

focus.cancel: On opening, the focus lands on Cancel: it comes first in the DOM on purpose, so that the keyboard lands on the safe answer.
focus.returns: The sheet asked to confirm that the focus returns the same way with Escape as with the button. It returns on all four ways out, and not because it is programmed here: it is the CDK’s restoreFocus, which does it for all of them. It is tested with Escape, which was the doubtful case.

name.ids: aria-labelledby points to the title and aria-describedby to the body. Both ids are minted by the service before opening, because the CDK configuration is put together before the component exists — generating them inside would have meant tampering with an internal CDK method.
name.test: The test does not check that the attributes are there: it checks that they resolve to elements that exist and that those say the title and the body.

aliases.blur: --backdrop-blur is the only blur value in the system, so backdrop-blur-dialog is the only blur utility that is emitted.
aliases.glyph: The glyph brings no token of its own: it is the family’s -text and the lg size of the icon scale. The halo and circle tokens were deleted on 2026-09-21.
aliases.radiusShadow: --radius-dialog comes from the length scale (the 20 px the sheet asks for) and --shadow-dialog from the same navy-7-a* as the rest of the scale: it is still tinted with the brand, not with grey.

mistakes.backdrop: Expecting the backdrop to close a Danger. It does not, and that is on purpose.
mistakes.component: Using the confirmation component directly. It is not exported: you call confirm(). A second way of raising a confirmation is how two confirmations in the same application end up different.
mistakes.focusTrap: Rebuilding the focus trap. It is already there. Every piece that looks trivial —what happens if whatever opened the dialog no longer exists when it closes, what happens if there is nothing focusable inside— is an edge case that a hand-made version gets wrong.
mistakes.notice: Opening a dialog to announce something. Use a Toast. A modal charges a click for a piece of news.

props.ariaLabelledBy: The id of the heading inside the component. Preferable to ariaLabel.

props.cancelLabel: Required. The text of the button that cancels. It comes first in the DOM, so that the keyboard lands there.

props.confirmLabel: Required. The text of the button that confirms. Already translated.
props.dismissOnBackdrop: It only governs the backdrop. Escape always closes, without exception.
props.injector: The injector of the screen that opens it: the component sees that screen’s texts and services. A form needs it. Without it, the root injector.

purpose.cdk: Built on @angular/cdk/dialog. The focus trap, the role, making the rest of the document inert and returning the focus on closing belong to the CDK and are not rebuilt here.
purpose.longForm: If the form is long, use a screen. A modal with its own scroll inside a page that scrolls means two scrolls and nowhere to go back to.
purpose.notice: If there is nothing to decide, use a Toast or a Banner. A modal to say “saved” makes people close something just for a piece of news.
purpose.reversible: If the action can be undone, it may not be needed. An undo is usually better than a confirmation: it does not interrupt the people who get it right.
purpose.solves: Stopping what is happening and asking for a decision. Two forms: a confirmation, which is a question with two answers and comes back as a Promise; and a form, which is a component the consumer provides.

keyboard.closeGlyph: A tab's “×” is not a tab stop, and that is deliberate. A tablist can only contain tabs: a real button in there is a critical axe violation. The way out is the APG's own one for deletable tabs — a non-focusable glyph for the mouse and Delete for the keyboard, announced with aria-keyshortcuts so it can be discovered. The function is available through both means, which is what 2.1.1 asks for; what there is not is a second stop per tab, and in a strip of twelve documents that is welcome.
keyboard.rail: The rail is ONE tab stop. WAI-ARIA APG treeview pattern: ↑↓ move through it, → opens a group or enters it, ← closes it or goes up to the parent, Home and End jump. With sixteen destinations, a tree where Tab visits every row costs sixteen presses just to get past it, on every screen.
keyboard.tabs: So are the tabs. ←→ move and select, Home/End jump, and Delete closes the active one if it is closable.

purpose.assembly: The assembly —wiring them to the router, to the real menu and to the permissions— is the App Shell, and it lives in the shell, not here.
purpose.groupNotDestination: A group is not a destination. An item with children opens. Making it navigate as well turns the answer to “what does this do?” into something that depends on where you clicked.
purpose.noRouter: None of them knows the router. They receive the items as an input, say which one is active and emit what was chosen. This very page proves it: there is not a single routerLink here, and all three work.
purpose.notBack: Breadcrumbs are not the “back” button. They show where you are in the hierarchy, not where you came through. If the path depends on how you got there, it is not a breadcrumb.
purpose.sectionCloses: mode="section" closes nothing. A subsection of a screen is not closed; what gets closed is a document.
purpose.solves: The three ways of moving around an application, as independent pieces: the menu tree, the tabs of what you have open and the path to where you are.

sizes.breakpoint: The breakpoint is a token and is read from TypeScript, not as a Tailwind md:. Mapping it into @theme emits @media (width >= var(--breakpoint-nav-bottom)), and a custom property is not substituted inside a media query: it compiles, nothing fails, and the layout never changes. Viewport reads it with readPixels, just as the Toast reads its duration.

messages.body: EWMS_PAGINATION_MESSAGES is provided once per application, like the table's or the select's: a screen with three paginators does not write the same dictionary three times. The [messages] input is optional and partial, and only overrides what an instance needs to say differently. Without a provider the control works all the same and stays silent. Inside a table there is nothing to pass: the paginator asks for its own.

mistakes.addOne: Adding one before passing it. page is the same number that travels in TableQuery. If the consumer has to add, someone is going to forget to subtract.
mistakes.noCount: Mounting it without knowing how many pages there are. Without pageCount there is no last end to disable.
mistakes.selfChange: Changing the page inside the component itself. It changes nothing on its own: it emits what it has been asked for and waits for the source to answer. A paginator that runs ahead shows a page that has not arrived yet.

props.caption: Properties of <ewms-pagination>
props.messages: Overrides, in this instance, the texts of EWMS_PAGINATION_MESSAGES (ADR 0008).
props.page: Required. The current page, counted from zero, as in TableQuery.
props.pageChange: The requested page, counted from zero. It changes nothing on its own.
props.pageCount: Required. How many pages there are. Without it the control is not mounted.
props.total: How many rows matched. With null nothing is said about the total.

purpose.jump: If you need to jump to a specific page, that does not exist yet. It is declared as a gap: the list of numbers is reported, not built.
purpose.noCount: If the source does not count, there is no paginator. With total: null there is no last page, and a control that hints at an end it does not know is lying.
purpose.scope: That is why it lives outside table/: it closes the gap the catalogue had kept reserved since DS-2, which the table is only the first to use.
purpose.solves: Moving through a set of results that does not fit all at once. Previous, next, and where you are. The table mounts it by itself when the source returns a total, but the component is independent: a list of cards, an event log or a picking queue paginate just the same and are not tables.
purpose.window: If the list is gone through in full, the window is the answer. Five thousand locations are looked at by scrolling, not by turning two hundred pages.

sizes.body: Both buttons are ewms-button iconOnly in sm. A paginator is a secondary control: it goes below the content, is used little and must not compete with what is being looked at. A configurable size would be an invitation to make it bigger than the table.

threshold.minKeystrokes: Besides the interval, it takes {{ count }} keys in a row below the threshold before a run counts as a scan. Two are not enough: two fast keys happen when someone types “SK” with both hands. A barcode never has two characters, so asking for four costs a real scan nothing.
threshold.proposal: --threshold-scan-keystroke is the only value that tells a person from a scanner gun, and it is a token precisely because the reader model on the warehouse floor is not known yet. Today's 50 ms are a reasoned proposal —a very fast human keeps up about 120 ms; an industrial reader is around 5–20— and not a measurement. Calibrating it against the real reader is a declared pending task, not an oversight.

outcomes.alreadyHandled: A closer component already answered it; the engine does not touch it again.
outcomes.burst: It arrived inside a scanner burst. No shortcut can act on it.
outcomes.deferred: It is a single key: the engine waits for a threshold to rule out a scan.
outcomes.inTextField: It is a shortcut, but the focus is in a text field and this one cannot fire there.
outcomes.key: It is not any key in the map. An ordinary key.
outcomes.scan: It closed a burst: the whole code is delivered, once, as an event of its own.
outcomes.singleKeyOff: It is a single-key shortcut and the WCAG 2.1.4 switch is off.
outcomes.unregistered: It is a shortcut in the map, but no screen registered that action.

props.host: Directive. The application's single listener, in the root layout. Mounting a second one throws instead of duplicating every shortcut.
props.isRegistered: Whether anyone is answering that action right now.
props.register: Says what this screen does with an action. From an injection context: the registration is withdrawn by itself when destroyed. Registering the same action twice throws.
props.scans: Every scan, with the complete code, once. Never loose keys.
props.singleKeyShortcuts: The WCAG 2.2 2.1.4 switch. When off, “/” and “?” stop acting; Alt+N and Ctrl+S carry on. In memory: the per-user preference depends on the backend.

purpose.byAction: A screen registers the action, never the key. The action → key map lives in a single file per application, and the ? help reads it: adding a shortcut does not mean touching the help.
purpose.notAPermission: It does not replace a permission check. A shortcut whose action the user cannot perform is simply not registered, and that authorises nothing: authorisation belongs to the backend.
purpose.notOneScreen: If it belongs to a single screen, it does not go here yet. This map covers the global shortcuts. Domain ones arrive with the first vertical domain (DS-6).
purpose.notTheOnlyWay: If the shortcut is the only way to do something, it is wrong. WCAG 2.1.1: everything a shortcut does must also be possible with Tab and Enter. The shortcut speeds things up; it does not replace the button.
purpose.scanner: And stops a barcode scanner gun, which presents itself to the system as a keyboard, from triggering any of them by accident. That is the requirement in charge: the failure mode is not an interface nuisance, it is a wrong stock movement.
purpose.solves: Lets the four actions an operator repeats all day —search, create, save, cancel— be done without leaving the keyboard, with the same keys throughout the application.

rules.burst: No key in a burst triggers a shortcut. And for the case the length of the run cannot catch —a code that starts with a shortcut key— single-character shortcuts wait for a threshold before acting. If another key arrives within that window, it was a scanner gun and the shortcut is cancelled.
rules.oneFile: The action → key map lives in a single file per application. Registering the same action twice throws; a registration is withdrawn by itself when its screen is destroyed.
rules.oneListener: A single listener in the whole application. Mounting a second [ewmsShortcutsHost] throws at start-up instead of silently duplicating every shortcut, and the code gate fails on any global keydown outside the engine.
rules.singleKey: Single-key shortcuts can be switched off from the help itself. It is WCAG 2.2 2.1.4 (Character Key Shortcuts), and the text-field rule does not cover it: it exists for people who use speech input, whose words become characters wherever the focus is. The preference lasts as long as the tab —remembering it needs a backend that does not exist yet.
rules.textField: No shortcut inside a text field, unless its binding says so. Today there are two: cancel, because half the times someone wants to cancel, the focus is inside the field they are filling in; and save, because Ctrl+S is pressed while typing in the form one wants to save.
rules.title: The five non-negotiable rules

sizes.modal: The only thing drawn is the help dialog, and it takes its box from the Modal: a single width, the geometry and the elevation that sheet already decided. A configurable size here would be a second Modal under another name.

The colours, the heights, the radii and the focus ring come whole from the components it composes —each with its sheet, its state matrix and its contrast already measured—. A pattern that needed tokens of its own would be a pattern remaking a component under another name.

contract.escape: Escape cancels in zero clicks and without asking. The CDK dialog closes it, and also marks the event as handled —and the engine does not respond to anything already handled—, so the screen behind does not cancel as well.

contract.scan: A scan selects without opening the panel and the table moves the focus to the row. It is the main use case of a WMS, and it is here and not only on the select’s sheet because here is where you can see that it triggers no shortcut along the way.
contract.search: Search can be reached from anywhere. The screen registers the search action; which key triggers it is none of its business.

purpose.notSheets: It does not apply to the catalogue sheets. The other 23 pages are documentation, not workflows: counting clicks on them would measure reading.
purpose.nothingNew: Nothing new was built here. Everything you see already existed: the searchable select and the table from DS-3, the dialog, the toast and the banner, and the shortcut engine from DS-4. That is the claim this page is here to make — that the budget is met by composing the system, not by solving it all over again on every screen.
purpose.onlyClicks: It measures neither time nor keystrokes. Only clicks, which is what the brief asks for. Time depends on the hardware on the warehouse floor, which is not known yet.
purpose.otherFlows: If the flow is not search, create or edit, the budget is not set. Approving, printing a label or transferring will get theirs when the screens that have them exist; giving them a number here would be making it up.
purpose.solves: It is the sample screen: the three operations an operator repeats all day long —search, create, edit— within an agreed click budget, measured right here.

sizes.sameScale: Each component brings its own and they all use the same control scale, which is what makes the search field and the “New” button next to it the same height without anybody having written it here.

cancelled.why: A “you changed your mind” notice is a notification about the absence of an event.

failing.why: It stays true until somebody fixes it. A toast would disappear, and whoever arrived four seconds late would never find out.

a11y.ariaChecked: aria-checked kept in sync with the state, so that it does not depend on colour.
a11y.fieldset:
The group is named with
and , as in the demo: each option's name says which option it is, and the group's says what is being chosen.
a11y.noAriaDisabled: No aria-disabled next to the native disabled: it would be announced twice.
a11y.wraps: The wraps the control, so the whole row is the clickable area and the text is the accessible name, with no for/id pair to maintain.

anatomy.caption: Tokens that <ewms-radio> consumes
anatomy.dot: The inner dot is a round , not an : it is a filled circle with no geometry, and an icon would be a whole SVG document to draw eight pixels.
anatomy.intro: Identical to the Checkbox's, and not because it was copied: both pages read the same constant, because both components read the same selection.types.ts. Only the corner radius and the glyph are written twice in the library.

contract.inputs: The five in the table in block 3. Two are required by the type: value and name.
contract.outputs: (valueChange), with this option's value. It is NOT called (change): that is a native event name, it bubbles, and an output that shares it delivers this value and the raw Event in the same binding.
contract.stopPropagation: And as in the Checkbox and the Toggle, the component calls stopPropagation() on the native change: the inner is an implementation detail and its events are not part of the API. Letting it out would mean publishing a second event that nobody documented and that the next internal change breaks.

demo.frame: A real group, inside a reactive form
demo.valueNote: value is what this option contributes when it is the chosen one; the control's value is the value of whichever option is chosen at that moment. That is why checked is derived by comparison and is not an input: two sources of truth for “is this the chosen one?” is exactly how a radio group ends up with two dots.
demo.valueNoteTitle: The group's value is NOT this component's value

disabledRule.form: Inside a form, what disables the group is the schema's disabled(path.tipo, …) rule, not an input: Angular forbids binding [disabled] on the same node as [formField], so that the field has a single owner.
disabledRule.or: isDisabled = disabled() || group.disabled(). Whoever disables wins, and nobody re-enables. The option's disabled and the group's are not merged: they are combined with OR.
disabledRule.safety: Disabling is a safety property: the restrictive answer is the right default. It is the same in the Checkbox, the Toggle, the Input and the Select.
disabledRule.title: The disabled rule

groupProps.caption: <ewms-radio-group> properties
groupProps.formState: From the FormValueControl contract. [formField] fills them in. None that the component does not read.
groupProps.hideLabelHint: As in the Input. The validator's message replaces the hint.
groupProps.label: Required. The legend of the fieldset. The group is what has a name, not each option.
groupProps.name: The name shared by the native radios, which IS the grouping. Without it, each instance gets its own: two groups never end up mixed.
groupProps.value: The field's value: the value of the chosen option. With [formField] the form fills it in; outside a form, [(value)].

mistakes.change: Listening to (change). It is (valueChange), and the native one is stopped inside.
mistakes.checked: Looking for a checked to write. There is none: it is derived by comparing the control's value with the option's value.
mistakes.enable: Setting [disabled]="true" and expecting form.enable() to bring it back. It does not.
mistakes.name: Forgetting the name, or repeating it across different groups. The first does not compile; the second makes two unrelated groups deselect each other.

radio.notApplicable: One: variants. It is written above rather than deleted.

props.ariaLabel: The accessible name when there is no visible text.
props.caption: <ewms-radio> properties
props.disabled: It is combined with the group's by OR, never subtracted: a disabled group switches off all its options.
props.label: Visible text next to the dot, already translated.
props.value: Required. What the GROUP's value becomes when this option is chosen. It is not the group's value: it is what this option contributes when it is the chosen one.

purpose.native: The grouping is the native one. Radios that share a name exclude each other because the browser does it, not because the component keeps a registry: selecting one deselects its siblings before a single line of Angular runs.
purpose.notClearable: If it must be possible to deselect, it is not a radio. A radio group does not go back to empty once something is chosen: that is a checkbox, or a select with a placeholder.
purpose.notMany: If there are many options, it is a Select. A list of fifteen radios is a screen you have to go through in full before deciding.
purpose.notMultiple: If more than one can be chosen, it is a Checkbox.
purpose.notWithoutName: Without a name it is not a radio, it is a radio in a group of one — in other words, a checkbox that cannot be switched off. That is why it is required.
purpose.solves: One option among several, mutually exclusive. The same 18×18 box, the same border, the same focus ring and the same row-as-clickable-area as the Checkbox; a circle instead of a rounded square, and a dot instead of a tick.

sizes.mismatch: The last two do not match: the token declares one and a half, and Chromium rounds a sub-pixel border down. What the component owes is the token; what the browser does with it is the browser's business. It is explained in more detail on the Checkbox sheet, which shares this very box.
sizes.single: 18×18 px, a 1.5 px border, an 8×8 inner dot. It does not use the 32 / 40 / 48 scale: it is sized to sit next to a line of text, not to line up with a button.
sizes.title: Just one, and it is the Checkbox's

states.caption: Two values by four states
states.hoverColumn: The Hover column only changes something in the first row, just as in the Checkbox: hover paints the border blue, and in “Chosen” the border is already blue. The cell is not broken; the state has nothing to add there.
states.intro: Two values by four states. Hover and Focus are forced with the same token their own rule would apply; Disabled is real, and on top of that it arrives through the form —setDisabledState— which is the half of block 8's OR that gets the least exercise.
states.ownGroup: Each cell is its own ewms-radio-group, with its own value. It is not ceremony: since checked is derived, a cell cannot be told to look chosen —it really has to be the chosen one in its group—; and if they all shared one value, clicking any “Not chosen” cell would light them all up at once. Each group generates its own name, so there is no need even to name them.

variants.none: There is no variant, just like the Checkbox. And unlike the Checkbox, there is no third value either: a radio is either chosen or it is not.
variants.onlyDifference: That absence is the only real difference in expression between the two selection controls, which otherwise share even the style file. The Checkbox has indeterminate because a checkbox can speak about a set of other things; a radio only speaks about itself.

a11y.announces: What each part announces: the field is role="combobox" with aria-haspopup="listbox" and aria-autocomplete="list"; its name is the visible label (through for/id) and its value is the label of what was chosen. A live region announces how many results there are. The panel is role="listbox" and each row role="option" with aria-selected.
a11y.controls: aria-controls exists only while the panel is in the document: pointing at an id that does not exist is an invalid value, and an invalid attribute is worse than a missing one.
a11y.focus: The focus never leaves the field. The panel is not focusable and nothing inside it is; the arrows move an active row and aria-activedescendant tells assistive technology which one it is. It is the ARIA Authoring Practices pattern for a combobox with a list, and it makes “the focus returns to the field on closing” true by construction rather than through a call to focus() that someone has to remember to fire on all four exits.
a11y.mousedown: A click on an option calls preventDefault() on mousedown, because that is where the focus moves, before the click. That is what keeps aria-activedescendant meaningful.
a11y.title: Accessibility: the keyboard, and what each part announces

contract.inputs: The ones in the table in block 3. label is the only one the type requires; options and source together are an error in development mode.
contract.messages: The search texts (searching, no results, error, retry, more) are not inputs: they are provided once through EWMS_SELECT_MESSAGES, which the shell fills with transloco; the catalogue uses those same ones. Without them the field works just the same, but the live region stays silent.

outputs.count: Two, and one of them is declared by model(): (valueChange) and (touch). The value travels through [formField] inside a form and through [(value)] outside one.
outputs.noChange:
And no native (change) leaks out: there is no browser and the panel a
    , so the event that does bubble —and that has to be stopped in the Checkbox, the Radio and the Toggle— simply does not exist here.
outputs.others: The other three selection controls do publish an output ((checkedChange), (valueChange)) as well as the form, because they have a native inside whose change has to be stopped. The Select has nothing to defend itself against.

contract.sourceContract: SearchSource is not an abstraction over an endpoint: it is the contract the catalogue endpoint has to meet (REQ-FE-DS3-001 RFE-02). Moving to a real backend changes that class and nothing else.
