keyboard.caption: The keyboard contract: a single one, on the field

enter.closed: Belongs to the form. After a scanner burst, it searches without waiting.
enter.open: Chooses the active row and closes.

escape.open: Closes without touching the value. It dismisses, and nothing more.

letters.closed: They type into the field and filter: instantly in memory, after the input delay against the source. Emptying the box does not clear the chosen value.

missing.body: There is no Home / End: it was never in the contract. The gap is documented instead of describing a keyboard the component does not have. When it searches, Enter with no active row belongs to the form: swallowing it would break submitting with the keyboard.
missing.title: What is NOT there

tab.open: Closes without choosing: the focus is on its way somewhere else.

mistakes.change: Looking for a (change). There is none, and no native one leaking out either: there is no browser
mistakes.disabled: Setting [disabled]="true" and expecting form.enable() to undo it. It does not: isDisabled = disabled() || disabledByForm(). Whoever disables wins, and nobody re-enables.
mistakes.escape: Expecting Escape to revert. It does not revert: it dismisses. The value the panel was showing stays exactly as it was, because closing does not go anywhere near the commit.
mistakes.labelAsValue: Passing the label as the value. What goes up to the form is value; the label is only what gets read.
mistakes.thousands: Loading thousands of options into memory. They filter, but they are all rendered on opening: a list of hundreds goes with source, which pages.

select.notApplicable: None. There are no emphasis variants, but block 4 shows the three forms it takes depending on where the options come from.

panel.flip: It flips upwards when it does not fit below. The list of positions has two entries and the CDK keeps the first one that fits. It is tested in the E2E, near the bottom edge.
panel.scroll: A long list scrolls inside the panel; that is not a limit on how many options can be passed, which the sheet forbids. Virtual scrolling for lists of more than a hundred is on the sheet and deliberately not built: it is an optimisation with no consumer yet.
panel.title: The panel: width and flip
panel.wFull: The list also carries w-full, and it is structural: the CDK's prebuilt stylesheet turns .cdk-overlay-pane into a flex container, and a flex item is sized by its content. Without it the list came out narrower than the field it belongs to — which is exactly what the first render of this code in a browser showed.
panel.width: The panel is as wide as the field, and the width is read on opening, not stored: the field changes width with the layout around it.

props.caption: Properties of <ewms-select>
props.display: label(item) and code(item). With display the value is the whole record.
props.errorDisabled: The first is visual; disabled is ORed with the form's.
props.hideLabel: The label leaves the view and stays for assistive technology, tied by for/id: the field and the list keep their name.
props.label: Required. Visible, tied to the field by for/id.
props.messages: Overrides, in a single instance, the texts from EWMS_SELECT_MESSAGES, which are provided once.
props.options: A closed list in memory: it opens in full and filters as you type, with no wait.
props.placeholderHint: Already translated. The hint goes through aria-describedby and turns danger with error.
props.size: The same scale as the Input and the Button: 32 / 40 / 48.
props.source: A backend source, paged. It rules out options: the two together are an error.
props.value: The chosen value. It seeds the control; after that, the form is in charge.
props.valueNote: What goes up to the form is the option's value, not its label. value is unknown on purpose: an id, a code, a member of an enum or a whole object are all legitimate, and narrowing it would force every consumer into a cast.

purpose.notInput: If the value can be typed freely, use Input. Searching filters a list; it does not accept text that is not in it.
purpose.notMulti: If several must be chosen, it does not exist yet. The multi-select with chips is on the sheet as pending.
purpose.notRadio: If there are two or three options that can be seen at a glance, use Radio. Hiding three options behind a click is extra work for whoever fills in the form.
purpose.scope: The box is the one from —same heights, padding, radius and borders— because a select nearly always sits in a row with an input and a button. The panel is an Angular CDK overlay, which flips when it does not fit below.
purpose.solves: A single choice, with a floating panel; it is the only picker in the system, and it always searches: it works for three statuses, for twenty locations and for tens of thousands of backend items, with the same field and the same keyboard.

searchStates.caption: The five search states, and what each one does

empty.value: Unchanged. A text with no matches does not clear what was chosen.
empty.where: A row in the panel, repeating the searched text.

error.value: Unchanged, and the typed text is not lost either.
error.where: A block below the field, in the flow, with a retry button.

idle.announce: Nothing: the live region is empty.
idle.where: Nothing. The panel is not in the document.

more.announce: “N of M” — or “N results” if the source does not count.
more.value: Unchanged until a row is chosen.
more.where: The last row of the panel, reachable with the arrows.

searching.where: A row with a spinner at the end of the panel.

searchStates.note: A table of facts rather than live components: five selects in a grid share a single overlay and none of them keeps still. They really break with the remote source buttons. “No results” and “service error” share neither the branch nor the place: mixing them up makes an outage look like an empty warehouse. The error goes in the flow, below the field, where one Tab reaches the retry.
searchStates.title: The search states

sizes.intro: Three heights, a single chevron size. Both are measured below.

why.rule: The reason is the rule the sheet itself states: “Select always uses the same scale as Input, so that mixed form rows can be aligned”. Scaling the chevron to 18 px in Large would break that alignment in exactly the row the rule exists to protect.
why.scale: The sheet asked for 14 / 16 / 18 px, and there is no 14: the system's icon scale is sm 16 / md 18 / lg 20 / xl 24. sm was fixed for all three, the same as the Input's prefix icon.
why.title: Why the chevron does not grow

states.caption: Four field states by three sizes
states.intro: The states of the closed field, against the three sizes. All twelve are real inputs: no cell is painted with a class.
states.missing: Focus and Open are missing, and for different reasons. Focus, for the same reason as in the Input: the border colour is an inline style tied to a component signal, and a wrapping class cannot beat it. Open, because it cannot be done: the panel lives in a CDK overlay outside the table, and there is only one.
states.openLikeFocus: Open also gets the same visual treatment as Focus, and that costs nothing: while the panel is up, the focus has not moved from the field.

hiddenLabel.body: With [hideLabel]="true" the label leaves the view and stays for assistive technology, tied by for/id as in the Input: the combobox and the list still have a name. It is for places where something visible already says it —the language switcher in the header, a filter next to its title—, not for saving space.
hiddenLabel.frame: A filter in a bar, with its title beside it
hiddenLabel.title: With the label hidden

variants.intro: There is no emphasis variant and no mode without search: the three demos above are the three forms, and they differ only in where the options come from.

notExact.body: If several match, or none, or the match is not exact, the panel opens with whatever there is and nothing is chosen. A person typing fast is not a scanner: the threshold is 50 ms per keystroke, and it is a proposal to be calibrated against the real reader, not a measurement.
notExact.title: And what happens when it is not exact

scanner.burst: A burst of keystrokes below the threshold, ending in Enter, is recognised as a scan and searches straight away. If a single record that matches exactly comes back, it is chosen without opening the panel. Zero clicks.
scanner.title: What happens with a scanner
scanner.tryIt: Try it by pasting <mono>{{ code }}</mono> into the item field and pressing Enter: a paste arrives as a burst, which is exactly what is being detected.

active.body: “The keyboard is here”: the same ghost-hover background the mouse produces, so that a list walked with the arrows looks the same as one walked with the pointer. It disappears on closing.
active.title: Active

selectedActive.both: A row is often both at once —on opening, the active row starts on the selected one— and that is why they get confused. They are two, and they are painted differently.

selected.body: “This is the current value”: text in action blue, semibold, and a check on the right. It survives closing the panel.
selected.title: Selected

selectedActive.title: Selected and active are independent

elevation.frame: On the canvas, which is where they live
elevation.intro: Derived from navy with alpha, not from grey or black: a shadow tinted with the brand colour blends in, a grey one looks dirty. There is no level above these three.
elevation.title: The three elevation levels

fixed.border: The border is 1.5, not 1: at 18×18 a border of 1 gets lost, and at 2 the box looks heavy next to the Input. It is the only border width in the system outside the whole-number scale.
fixed.box: An 18×18 box, in a single size. A checkbox is not sized to line up with a button: it is sized to sit next to a line of text.
fixed.intro: Three measurements in the system that do not come from the control scale. They are here, and not in each component's sheet, because they are facts about the system's geometry just like the heights above — and because until now nobody had measured them in a browser.
fixed.title: The geometries that do not scale
fixed.toggle: A 44×24 track with the 20 thumb set 2 in from each end: 2 + 20 + 2 is exactly the height of the track, and 20 of travel leaves it the same distance from the other side.

header.intro: The whole spacing scale comes from a single multiplier. There is no list of values: there is a base, and Tailwind derives the rest. Changing the base moves the entire application and breaks no proportion.

heights.intro: Button, Input and Select share the three heights by rule, not by coincidence: a form mixes all three in the same row, and they have to line up.
heights.title: The three control heights

mixed.intro: A real Input, Select and Button, all three in Medium. It is the check on the rule: the boxes measure the same, but the horizontal padding is not the same in all three (10/12/14 in the fields against 12/16/20 in the button), so what to look at is whether the text sits at the same optical height.
mixed.selectNote: The Select opens here: it is a panel in the CDK overlay, and until this page none had ever been rendered.
mixed.title: The mixed row

radii.signature: The system's visual signature. It is the radius that Button, Input and Select share, which is why a control with any other radius looks out of place straight away.
radii.title: The five radii

uses.control: Button, Input and Select. The same one for all three, always.
uses.full: The Toggle's track and thumb, avatars.

scale.intro: A p-4 utility is four times that base, and gap-2 is two. The bars below are drawn with those same utilities: what you see is the real scale, not an illustration of the scale.
scale.title: The base, and what comes out of it

a11y.keys: Enter, Space and ↓ open on the first option; ↑, on the last. The focus enters the menu and aria-activedescendant marks the option; Esc closes it and returns the focus to the arrow.
a11y.pattern: APG menu button pattern: the arrow is a button with a name (the moreActions of EWMS_SPLIT_BUTTON_MESSAGES), aria-expanded and aria-controls.

anatomy.noToken: No token of its own: the inner corners are squared off and the border between the two is drawn only once. The menu is <mono>lib/menu/</mono>, the same one as the Table’s.

parts.border: Border, a single one between the two

demo.frame: Exporting a list of shipments
demo.keyboard: Try it with the keyboard: Tab to the arrow, <kbd>↓</kbd> opens on the first option, the arrows move through them skipping “Labels”, <kbd>Enter</kbd> chooses and <kbd>Esc</kbd> closes, returning the focus to the arrow.

splitButton.notApplicable: Variants and sizes: written above rather than deleted.

props.action: The id of the alternative chosen in the menu.
props.actions: '{ id, label, icon?, disabled? }'. A disabled one is visible and the arrows skip it.
props.caption: Properties of <ewms-split-button>
props.icon: Icon of the main action, from the closed catalogue.
props.label: Required. Text of the main action, already translated. It also names the menu.
props.primary: The main action: the button with text.

purpose.mixedVerbs: If the menu mixes verbs (“Download”, “Delete”), it is the row menu, not a split: here everything is the same action in a different form.
purpose.sameWeight: If the alternatives carry the same weight, there is no main action: use separate buttons or a Select.
purpose.solves: An action that is almost always used the same way, with alternatives one click away: “Download” gets the PDF, and the arrow offers Excel or CSV. It is two joined together; the menu is the same one as in the Table row.

sizes.height: 40 px, the default control height: it lives in toolbars next to other Medium buttons. A configurable size will come when a consumer asks for it.
sizes.title: Does not apply — Medium

states.halves: Each half is a Secondary , with its hover, focus, disabled and loading states, which are in the Button’s matrix. When open, the arrow announces aria-expanded="true".
states.title: The Button’s own

variants.title: Does not apply — always Secondary
variants.why: A split offers a choice; the main action of the screen is a different one, and it is Primary. Two Primary buttons side by side no longer say which one is the main one.

detail.intro: The chevron opens a panel as wide as the table; the kebab opens the menu, and right-clicking the row opens the same menu. From the keyboard: Shift+F10 or the menu key, arrows to move through it, and Escape returns the focus to the row.
detail.title: Detail and row menu

deviation.cdk: The brief asked for cdk-virtual-scroll-viewport. That component positions its content with a transform and measures the wrapper: wrapping a moves the whole table —header included— and the sticky header stops sticking. The CDK’s own guidance is to virtualise a list of divs, which here would mean giving up table semantics: the header/cell relationship and the row and column counts. For a table an operator lives in for eight hours, that trade goes the wrong way.
deviation.title: Declared deviation: the window is our own, not the CDK’s
deviation.window: So the window is worked out here, and it is short because the tree is already flattened: the scroll offset divided by the row height gives the first row, the height of the box gives how many, and two spacer rows hold the scrollbar up. It is reported, not done quietly.

gestures.notARow: The panel does not count as a row. It is in the DOM, but aria-rowcount still says how many shipments there are: if it counted, opening a detail would make the table “grow” to the ears of a screen reader.
gestures.rowsOrPanel: A parent unfolds more rows, in the same columns. A master row unfolds a panel, with content of its own that does not repeat the columns. A single control that sometimes did one thing and sometimes the other would be a control nobody can predict, so they are two different buttons and a table can have both.
gestures.title: Detail and tree are two gestures, not one

advanced.intro: What the main demo does not show: the detail panel, the row menu, children that take a while to arrive, five thousand rows and the paginator. Each one with its own synthetic source.

lazy.frame: Lazy loading of children, with its error state
lazy.intro: [children] as a function that returns an Observable. The shipment with an issue always fails: you see the error row and its retry button. The consumer writes neither of the two states.
lazy.title: Children that arrive late, and sometimes not at all

pagination.intro: When the source returns a total, the table mounts . If the total is null —a source that does not count— there is no paginator, because a paginator with no last page lies about how far it goes.
pagination.title: Pagination

advanced.title: Advanced composition

virtual.intro: [virtual]="true" draws only what can be seen. aria-rowcount still says how many rows there really are, and the arrow keys walk the whole table: the window is an implementation detail and the keyboard should not notice it.
virtual.sample: The demo starts with a sample of sixty and loads the five thousand when asked to: a catalogue sheet that builds five thousand rows the moment it opens is slow for everyone, whether or not they look at this demo.
virtual.title: Five thousand locations, windowed

anatomy.caption: Tokens that <ewms-table> consumes
anatomy.collapsed: A collapsed row is not in the DOM; it is not hidden with CSS. A row that is not in the DOM cannot be reached with Tab, is not read by a screen reader and does not count towards aria-rowcount — and all three would be wrong for something the person collapsed.
anatomy.flatTitle: The tree is flattened, and that is why there is a single loop
anatomy.flattenTree: flattenTree() is a pure function, with no Angular, no signals and no DOM, tested on its own: given the roots, how to find children and the set of expanded rows, it returns the array the template walks.

parts.hoverRow: Row on hover and with focus
parts.maxHeight: Maximum height: the header stays put
parts.pinShadow: Shadow of a pinned column with content underneath

anatomy.toggle: The toggle lives inside the first data column, next to the text, never in a column of its own; a row without children gets a .tree-toggle-spacer of the same width so that the text of every row starts in the same place. It is the vocabulary set by the Naming convention.
anatomy.virtualise: That is also what will make it possible to virtualise without tricks: the CDK needs a flat list of known length, and there already is one.

colour.badge: Every row coloured by state also carries its badge, with an icon and with words. Someone who cannot tell the four tints apart still reads “With issue”, and so does someone using a screen reader.
colour.icons: The icons are the same four that the Banner and the Toast use: someone who learnt that the crossed-out circle means an error in a toast has to find it meaning the same in a row.
colour.title: Colour is never the only signal (WCAG 1.4.1)

columnTypes.caption: The type decides four things at once
columnTypes.title: The five column types

keyboard.caption: A single Tab stop for the whole table
keyboard.enter: (rowActivate). A double click does the same: two paths, one action.
keyboard.homeEnd: First or last cell of the row. With <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>, of the table.
keyboard.left: On an expanded parent row, it collapses. Otherwise, previous cell; on the first cell of a child, it goes to the parent row.
keyboard.right: On a collapsed parent row, it expands. Otherwise, next cell.
keyboard.space: Toggles the row’s selection. It also stops the scroll, which is the last thing someone marking rows wants.
keyboard.title: Keyboard — the treegrid pattern, followed rather than reinvented
keyboard.upDown: Previous or next row, same column.

notAField.output: Its selection is an output, not a form value: what a table holds is a query, not a field, and binding it with [formField] would be a category error.
notAField.title: The table is NOT a form field
notAField.trackBy: The selection is kept as a set of ids by trackBy, not of objects: that way it survives a change of page, which is exactly when a selection kept by reference gets lost without warning.

contract.outputs: None is named like something native: (rowActivate) and not (dblclick), (rowMenu) and not (contextmenu), (selectionChange) and not (change). It is the rule that has already bitten three times in this system.

demo.componentLines: lines: the source, how a row is identified, the status dictionary, and the bulk actions with what each one does, which is screen logic and not table logic.
demo.frame: The real component, with its source in memory
demo.intro: Expand a shipment, and then a line. Header → line → serial number or lot. Twelve synthetic shipments generated from a seed, always the same ones; no real data from any customer.
demo.lastQuery: What the last query asked for:
demo.noFunctions: There is no state function and no children function: both are property names, and the state dictionary was already written for the badge column.
demo.templateLines: lines, counted by reading the block above from the DOM — not typed in by hand.
demo.templateTitle: The template that produced it, exactly as written
demo.title: Main demo — shipments, three levels
demo.underCeiling: under the ceiling of 40 set by the brief

columns.text: Drag the header, or use Alt+Shift+←/→ with the focus on it, or Move up/Move down in View. Each header’s ⋮ (or Shift+F10) sorts, pins, fits to content, moves and hides. Everything leaves through (viewChange), and “Reset view” undoes it.
columns.title: Columns: reorder, pin, fit

emptyState.text: With no filters, “no rows yet”; with any, “no rows match” with “Clear filters”; if the source fails, “Retry”. Search for something that does not exist in the demo.
emptyState.title: An empty state that chooses for itself

export.text: A CSV of everything filtered and sorted, with a BOM so that Excel reads the accents; or only the selection, or to the clipboard. With a remote source the table does not download: it emits (exportRequest).
export.title: Export

hiddenFilters.text: The filter row is hidden: “Filters” shows it (or <kbd>Alt+R</kbd> with the focus on the table). Hiding it clears nothing: each active filter stays as a chip, and its × removes it. The toolbar is four controls: search, Filters, View and Export.
hiddenFilters.title: Filters that tuck away

differentiators.intro: All of them are in the demo above and none of them asks for template: each one is switched on with an attribute of the table or of a column. What the user configures lives in memory and leaves through an output.

multiSort.text: A click sorts by one; <kbd>Shift+click</kbd> adds another, and the header shows its priority. The query carries the whole list.
multiSort.title: Sorting by several columns

polish.text: Only the exceptions tint the row, with a side bar that survives selection; numbers and dates with aligned digits; truncated text shows in full on hover or on focus; the shadow of what is pinned appears only when there is something underneath.
polish.title: Polish and states

selection.text: Shift+click marks a range; the toolbar says how many and offers the bulk actions. <kbd>Ctrl+C</kbd> copies what is marked, or the row with focus, ready to paste into Excel.
selection.title: Selection with intent

setFilter.text: Status is filtered with checkboxes from its dictionary, with an indeterminate “All”: “With issue” plus “In progress” is two clicks. [filterable] on a badge column.
setFilter.title: Set filter

statusBar.text: At the foot: how many rows, how many are selected, and Packages added up (aggregate="sum") over the selection if there is one, or over what is on screen.
statusBar.title: Status bar and aggregates

differentiators.title: The differentiators, one by one

filterByType.empty: An empty box means “no limit”, never zero. “Up to 50” is a maximum with no minimum, and reading the empty box as 0 would quietly throw away every row below it.
filterByType.range: A range typed into a text box is a filter that cannot compare: every source would have to interpret “100-900”, and each one would interpret it differently. A number column sends two numbers and a date column sends two ISO dates. That is what travels in TableQuery, and that is what the backend will be asked for.
filterByType.title: The type decides the filter, and the consumer configures nothing

formatting.locale: Formatting a date or a quantity requires a locale, and the design system speaks no language (ADR 0008). So it defines EWMS_TABLE_FORMATTERS and does not implement it: the shell fills it from core/i18n with transloco-locale, and this catalogue —which cannot import core— fills it with Intl. The same component, two implementations behind the same interface.
formatting.rawValue: Sorting and filtering always work on the raw value. The formatter decides how it looks and nothing more: a column of numbers with [1200, 900] sorts 900, 1200 even though the screen says 1,200 and 900. Sorting by the formatted text is the mistake that makes people stop trusting the column.
formatting.title: The table does not format: it asks for the format

log.bulkChoice: {{ action }} · {count, plural, one {# shipment} other {# shipments}}

mistakes.cellTemplate: Using ewmsCell for everything. It is the way out for the unusual. Five types cover what a WMS table really shows, and each one brings its cell, its alignment and its filter.
mistakes.formatBefore: Formatting the value before passing it. Then sorting and filtering work on the text, and 1,200 comes before 900. The formatter is for looking, not for comparing.
mistakes.selectAll: Expecting “select all” to reach what cannot be seen. It selects what is on screen. Reaching rows nobody looked at is how four hundred records get deleted when the aim was to delete twenty.
mistakes.toggleColumn: Putting the tree toggle in a column of its own. It lives inside the first data column. A column just for the toggle throws the text of every row out of line.
mistakes.twoDictionaries: Passing the state dictionary twice. With rowState="estado", the tint is read from the same badge column. A second dictionary is a second place where the two can contradict each other.

table.notApplicable: One: variants, because the table has no visual variants. It is written above rather than deleted.

props.ariaLabel: Required. Names the grid. A table with no name is a table nobody can ask for.
props.bulkAction: The chosen bulk action, with the selected rows from any page.
props.bulkActions: Actions on the selection; the toolbar shows them next to “3 selected”.
props.caption: Properties of <ewms-table>
props.children: A function, or the name of a property. With it there is a tree and the role is treegrid; without it, grid.
props.columnChooser: Column chooser in the toolbar. The last visible column cannot be hidden.
props.columnExtras: Initial pinning (the user changes it in the ⋮ menu), no checkbox in View, or the total at the foot.
props.density: The density it starts with; after that it is chosen in the toolbar. Row height by token.
props.exportRequest: Only with a remote source: the table does not download, it says what the user asked for.
props.exportable: Export: CSV on the client with ArrayTableSource; with a remote source, (exportRequest).
props.pageSize: How many root rows each query asks for.
props.queryChange: The whole query on every change (sorting is a list): what a saved view will persist.
props.quickFilter: The global search field above the table.
props.rowActivate: Double click and Enter. Two paths, one action. It is not called (dblclick).
props.rowState: A function, or the name of a badge column: then one dictionary feeds both the tint and the badge.
props.selectable: A checkbox column, with the indeterminate state in the header.
props.selectionChange: The selection. An output, not a form value: the table is not a CVA.
props.source: Required. Where the rows come from. An interface: the table knows nothing about HTTP.
props.trackBy: Identifies the row, AND the selection too: that is why the selection survives a change of page.
props.viewChange: Sorting, hidden columns, widths, pinned columns and density: in memory, for whoever wants to save them.

purpose.notCard: If it is three facts about one record, use Card. A one-row table is a record card with headers to spare.
purpose.notEditing: If cells have to be edited in place, it does not exist yet. It is declared as a gap: in-cell editing, grouping by column and export are reported, not built.
purpose.notPicker: If one record has to be picked out of thousands, use the searchable select. Walking a table with the arrow keys to find a SKU is exactly the case that component exists to avoid.
purpose.rule: The rule it was written by fits on one line: a lot of capability, little code in the consumer. What you see below is {{ lines }} lines of template.
purpose.solves: It is where an operator lives eight hours a day. Rows with hierarchy, states at a glance, sorting, per-column filters, multiple selection and a keyboard that never forces a reach for the mouse.

rowMatrix.caption: Background and mark of each row state
rowMatrix.intro: Background and mark of each state, with the classes the table uses. Selected wins over the tint; the exception keeps its side bar. AA contrast measured for the text and the badges on each background (in the sheet).
rowMatrix.title: The row matrix

sizes.caption: The row height, read from the token

controlHeight.text: And not by chance: a cell has to be able to hold an without the row growing. The E2E measures both and asserts that they match, which is the only way for it to still be true six months from now.
controlHeight.title: The medium row height is the height of the md control

sizes.intro: Two densities. They are chosen in the “View” panel of the table’s toolbar; density is the value it starts with.

states.caption: Each state, and the two signals it produces
states.disabled: Disabled is not in the matrix, and it is not a gap: a row cannot be disabled, because a row is not a control. Hover and focus are above, with their background; in the demo you can really move through them.
states.intro: The four row states, with the signals each one produces, all from the same dictionary. Only the exceptions tint the row —“With issue” and “In progress”—; the rest carry only the badge. With every row tinted, none of them stood out.

variants.naming: The system’s naming convention says so: the table does not follow the Componente/Variante/Tamaño/Estado pattern because it has no variants. What it does define are two sub-vocabularies: the row classes and the status badge.
variants.title: Does not apply — the table has no visual variants

a11y.axe: axe's heading-order rule runs with no tag filter in the harness, so a skipped level blows up gate 5. Where it really bites is at page level: an isolated component has almost nothing to compare itself with, which is why the E2E walks the whole showroom.
a11y.judgement: What no tool sees: whether the outline of a new screen makes sense. The coupling stops anyone from lying on purpose; it is no substitute for looking at it.
a11y.semantic:
The rendered element is the semantic level. No role is added on top: an

is already a level 3 heading, and giving it the role only adds a second source of truth.
a11y.spans: caption and mono render : they are not headings and do not appear in the outline.

anatomy.font: The typeface is self-hosted Montserrat, variable 100–900. It is not loaded from a CDN: the CSP only allows font-src 'self', and it also avoids leaking the IP addresses of the people who use the application.
anatomy.measuredIntro: Read from the DOM of this very page, not transcribed. If someone added an as, this table would be the first thing to stop matching the one above.
anatomy.renderedCaption: Rendered element and computed size, by variant
anatomy.tokensIntro: Size, weight and line height, read live. Four are still undecided in tokens.css and are marked as such: a visible gap is information, an invented number is not.

contract.inputs: Just one, variant, and it is input.required(). No default, on purpose: choosing the level is the decision this component forces you to make, and a default value would hide it.
contract.outputs: None. It is a presentation primitive: there is nothing to emit.

demo.confirm: The operator confirms the quantity received before closing the receipt. Until then the order stays open and accepts corrections.
demo.frame: A real block, with its full hierarchy
demo.outline: That block is exactly what a screen reader sees when it lists the headings: <mono>h2 → h3 → h4</mono>, with no jumps, because there is no way to write it otherwise.
demo.packagesStatus: Three packages declared, two verified. The third went into quarantine.

mistakes.handWritten:
Writing

by hand because “it is the same”. It is not: there nothing forces the level to match the appearance, and the day someone changes the size, the structure stays as it was.
mistakes.smallTitle: Using h4 as a “small title”. If what you need is a label above a piece of data, it is caption. The h4 goes into the document outline and a screen reader will list it as a heading.
mistakes.uppercase: Writing the text already in capitals for the h4. The CSS adds them. The text node keeps its original capitalisation, which is what makes the screen reader read it as a word and not letter by letter.

text.notApplicable: Two, written above rather than deleted: state matrix (the component has no states) and sizes (the size is the variant).

props.caption: Properties of <ewms-text>
props.content: Projected text. The text, already translated by the consumer: the design system speaks no language.
props.variant: Required. Sets size, weight and line height at once, and determines the element that is rendered. It has no default: choosing the level is THE decision, and a default would hide it.

purpose.coupling:
It exists so that visual hierarchy and document structure cannot be separated: variant="h2" looks like an H2 and is an

. Always. A screen that writes

by hand has bypassed the system, and nothing forces its level to match what is seen.
purpose.noAs: There is no as. There is no way to look like one level and be another. It was considered and ruled out: an escape hatch that is always used stops being an escape hatch, and ends up breaking the outline with a prop that looks as if it had been thought through.
purpose.notAHeading: If the right level does not look the way you want, it almost certainly was not a heading. The case that prompted as —the title of a KPI card, “PENDING RECEIPTS” above a big number— is a label, and it takes caption.
purpose.outline: The uncomfortable corollary is functional: people who navigate with a screen reader jump from heading to heading. An outline that lies is a screen that cannot be navigated.
purpose.scale: This is not the page for seeing the scale. The sizes at full size are in Foundations / Typography. This page documents the component.
purpose.solves: It is the only legitimate way to set text in the system's style. A variant sets all three things at once —size, weight and line height— and also decides which element is rendered.

samples.p: The operator confirms the quantity before closing.

sizes.noSize: There is no size. The size is the variant: they are not combined separately, and that is precisely the coupling the component lives on. A size on top of variant would be as through the back door.
sizes.scale: The full scale, at actual size and with its context of use, is in Foundations / Typography.

states.caption: Seven variants: which element they produce and how they look
states.coupling: What does vary —and it is the only thing this component exists to couple— is the pair document element versus appearance. That is the grid below: reading a row from left to right is the argument for the whole component.
states.measured: The middle column is not written by hand: it is the tagName the browser reported for each sample in the variants block, the same one listed in Anatomy. If someone added an as, this column would stop matching the one on the left — which is the only way a grid can demonstrate a coupling instead of asserting it.
states.none: has no states: no hover, no focus, no disabled. It is a primitive that renders an element and stops there.
states.title: The state matrix does not apply — and it is written out anyway

variants.intro: Seven, and they are semantic: they name what the text is for, not how big it is. Four render headings, one renders a paragraph and two render — caption and mono are not headings and must not appear in the document outline.
variants.uppercase: The capitals of h4 are applied by the component with text-transform, never by the dictionary text: a screen reader spells out a word written in capitals, and text that is already capitalised cannot be recapitalised according to the language.

a11y.escape: Escape is listened for on the document, because a toast never has the focus: it is not a tab stop and must not steal the focus from what the operator is doing. An Escape that something else has already handled —a dialog's, the Select's— is let through.
a11y.oneRegion: A single live region, always in the document, whether it is empty or not. A region that appears together with its first message is announced inconsistently —several screen readers miss content that arrives in the same frame as the region—, so the region waits and the only thing that changes is its content.
a11y.polite: polite and never assertive: a toast reports something that has already happened. What truly cannot wait is a Banner with role="alert", which is the other component.
a11y.severity: Each icon carries the severity as its accessible name, in the same words the consumer translated when mounting the outlet. Colour is not the only cue.

stack.clicks: The container does not catch clicks —the toasts do—, so that corner of the screen stays usable when there is nothing in the queue.
stack.corner: Bottom right — and the sheet does not say so: it says “floating” and nothing more. It is reported as a finding rather than written into the sheet on our own initiative. Meanwhile it is the corner furthest from what an operator is reading, and the one that does not cover the header.
stack.layer: The stack is drawn above the content and below the CDK overlay container. A toast raised while a dialog is open stays behind it, on purpose: the dialog is modal, and a message floating on top invites a click that the modal exists to prevent.
stack.title: Where it stacks, and why beneath a dialog

contract.translated: The text arrives already translated. The design system speaks no language (ADR 0008), and that holds for a service just as much as for a component.

demo.escape: Escape closes the most recent one. It is the only way to remove one by hand: the toast has no close button, and that leaves open —on purpose— the pending item the sheet declares.
demo.frame: Real queue, real outlet
demo.intro: Press a button, and watch the bottom right-hand corner. These buttons call the real ToastService, and the messages come out through the only outlet in the document, the one in the shell. This page does not mount a second one: two live regions would announce every message twice.
demo.sticky: One that does not go away on its own
demo.stickyMessage: No connection to the print server. This one does not go away on its own: close it with Escape.

mistakes.actionButton: Putting an action button inside. It does not exist and is not planned. An “undo” inside something that goes away on its own after three seconds is a race against the clock.
mistakes.closeButton: Expecting a close button. There is none either: the sheet declares it pending and this piece of work does not resolve it. Escape closes the most recent one.
mistakes.errorToFix: Using it for an error that has to be fixed. That calls for a Banner: it stays.
mistakes.secondOutlet: Mounting a second outlet. There is no guard in the code to prevent it: the rule holds because of where it is written, one line in the shell layout. Two outlets are two live regions, and every message announced twice.

toast.notApplicable: One: sizes, because the toast has only one. It is written above rather than deleted.

props.caption: ToastService methods, and the two inputs of <ewms-toast-outlet>
props.clear: Empties the queue, timers included. It is called automatically when the injector is destroyed.
props.dismiss: Removes one. An id that is no longer there is not an error.
props.dismissLatest: Removes the most recent one. It is what Escape does.
props.regionLabel: Required. An outlet input. It names the live region, so that the screen reader says where the message comes from.
props.severityLabels: Required. An outlet input. The four severities in words, for the accessible name of each icon. They are translated once, where the outlet is mounted.
props.show: Queues a message and returns its id. duration in milliseconds overrides the token for that call; 0 means “never expires”.
props.toasts: What the outlet renders, from oldest to newest.

purpose.decide: If a decision is needed, use a Dialog. A toast has no buttons and never will: it is not a place where you act.
purpose.mustRead: If it has to be read no matter what, a toast that goes away on its own is the wrong choice. You can pass duration: 0, but think twice: a fixed message in a corner is a misplaced Banner.
purpose.service: It is a service, not a component you put in the template: it is called from code, and the outlet is already mounted once in the root layout.
purpose.solves: Telling people something that has just happened without interrupting what they are doing. It floats, stacks with the others and goes away on its own. It does not shift the layout and asks for nothing.
purpose.stillTrue: If the condition is still true, use a Banner. An “aisle blocked” toast disappears after three seconds, and whoever arrived four seconds late never found out.

duration.caption: The default time, read live from the token
duration.title: What is a number: how long it lives

sizes.fits: There is no size. The toast grows with its message up to a maximum width and wraps there; the only fixed things are the 4 px accent and the 18 px icon.

fromTs.noFallback: And there is no fallback number. If the stylesheet is not loaded, the read comes back empty and the toast does not expire: it stays until someone closes it. A fallback written in the code is a second source of truth in disguise, which is right until the day the token moves. A message that stays too long is a nuisance; one that disappears after a time nobody declared is a bug nobody finds.
fromTs.readsIt: A colour or a radius is consumed as a utility or as var() and never reaches the code. A time does: it is an argument to setTimeout. So the service reads it from the document instead of copying it.
fromTs.title: It is the first token a component reads from TypeScript

states.noInteraction: Nor is there Hover, Focus or Disabled: a toast is not pressed, does not receive focus and cannot be disabled. Its only state of its own is being there or not being there.
states.samples: These cells are token samples, not live toasts, and that is the honest way to draw this grid. A toast lives in a single floating stack in a corner of the viewport: eight of them cannot be held still inside a table. The real component is above, in the demo, where it actually lives.

accent.solid: It is also the first consumer of the solid family, which the sheet had noted as unused.

a11y.ariaChecked: aria-checked kept in sync with the state: the state never depends on colour.
a11y.ariaDisabled: No aria-disabled next to the native disabled: it would be announced twice.
a11y.native: The element underneath is still an , so the space bar operates it, it joins the tab order and it gets the focus ring on the element that really has the focus. The only thing that had to change was the role.
a11y.switch: role="switch", never role="checkbox", however much it resembles one. A checkbox is announced as “checked / not checked” —the vocabulary of a selection— and a switch as “on / off”, which is what this control really does.

anatomy.caption: Tokens that <ewms-toggle> consumes
anatomy.intro: The track is the , with appearance-none; the thumb is an overlaid sibling with pointer-events-none, because an cannot have children and every pointer event belongs to the control underneath.

noSlide.body: And it is on purpose. This library has no duration token, and the theme removes Tailwind's, so an animation utility here would compile, apply a literal zero and look exactly like this while pretending otherwise. Adding the slide starts with adding a token, not with adding a class.
noSlide.title: The thumb does not slide — it jumps to the other side

contract.inputs: The four in the table in block 3. None is required by the type, but one of label or ariaLabel is in practice: without either, the switch has no accessible name.
contract.outputs: (checkedChange), the same name as in the Checkbox. NOT (change): it is a native event name and it bubbles, so an output with that name delivers this component's boolean and the raw Event in a single binding.
contract.stopPropagation: The component also calls stopPropagation() on the native change: the inside is an implementation detail and its events are not part of the API.

demo.frame: Preferences: each row applies when touched
demo.hitTarget: The whole row is the clickable area, not the 44×24 track: the wraps the control. On a tablet, inside a warehouse and wearing gloves, that is the difference between a control that works and one that does not — and that is where this control is really used.
demo.intro: A preferences panel. There is no Save button anywhere, and that absence is deliberate: the counter below goes up the very instant you touch a switch.

disabledRule.form: For the form to handle it, do not pass the input: the schema rule does the rest. Identical in the Checkbox, the Radio, the Input and the Select.
disabledRule.owner: One owner at a time. Outside a form, the disabled input. Inside one, the schema's disabled(path.x, …) rule.
disabledRule.title: The disabled rule
disabledRule.why: They are not combined because Angular does not allow it: binding [disabled] on the same node as [formField] is a compile error (NG8022). Disabling is a safety property, and with a single owner there are never two sources in disagreement.

mistakes.change: Listening to (change). It is (checkedChange); the native one is stopped inside.
mistakes.disabledTrue: Setting [disabled]="true" and expecting form.enable() to bring it back. It does not.
mistakes.roleCheckbox: Using role="checkbox" because “it is a checkbox inside”. It is one inside precisely so that nothing has to be reimplemented; what is announced is something else.
mistakes.save: Putting a Save button next to it. If the change needs confirming, the control should have been a Checkbox.
mistakes.slide: Expecting the thumb to slide. It does not, and adding it starts with a duration token.

toggle.notApplicable: One: variants. It is written above rather than deleted.

props.ariaLabel: The accessible name where there is no room for visible text.
props.caption: Properties of <ewms-toggle>
props.checked: Seeds the state. After that the form rules, just as in the Checkbox.
props.checkedChange: The same name as in the Checkbox, and for the same reason: (change) is native and bubbles.
props.disabled: Outside a form. Inside one it is set by the schema's disabled() rule — see block 8.
props.label: Visible text next to the switch, already translated. The whole row is the hit target.

purpose.destructive: If the action is destructive or costly, not that either: applying on touch without confirmation is not what you want for “Decommission the warehouse”.
purpose.native: Underneath it is still an , because the only thing that needed changing was the role: the keyboard, the focus and the tab stop were already right.
purpose.save: If there is a “Save” next to it, use Checkbox. That is the whole rule, and it is the most common confusion in this library. If your demo has a Save button next to a toggle, the demo is wrong.
purpose.solves: A switch: on or off, applied the moment it is touched. There is no Save button, because there is nothing left to save.
purpose.threeStates: If there are three states —yes, no, inherited— it is not a switch. That is a Select or a group of Radios.

sizes.arithmetic: It does not use the 32 / 40 / 48 scale, just like the Checkbox and the Radio. The arithmetic is 2 + 20 + 2 = 24: the thumb is inset 2 px from the top and 2 px from the left, and 20 px of travel leave it the same 2 px from the other end.
sizes.measuredNote: Measured on the rendered control, not transcribed: the sheet says 44×24 and 20, and that is exactly the kind of number that breaks without anyone noticing.
sizes.title: Just one — 44×24, with a 20 thumb

states.caption: Two values by four states
states.disabled: Disabled comes first and has no hover: a switch that cannot be operated must not light up under the pointer.
states.hover: The hover depends on the row, not the column: off moves to a darker border grey, on to a darker action blue. They are two different tokens, which is why the forced utility is chosen by value and not by state.
states.intro: Eight cells: two values by four states. Disabled is a real input; Hover and Focus are forced with the token the component's own rule would apply.

variants.none: There is no variant. A switch has two positions and no hierarchy of emphasis: there is no such thing as “the primary toggle”.
variants.values: What there is, is two values, Off and On, and they are the axis of the matrix.

versus.checkbox: A selection inside a form, confirmed later by something else.
versus.cost: Getting it wrong is not cosmetic: a toggle inside a form leaves a setting already applied while a Save button suggests it is not; a checkbox used for an immediate setting silently discards the change when someone leaves the screen without submitting.
versus.title: Toggle or Checkbox — the difference is not how they look
versus.toggle: Immediate action. It takes effect the moment it is touched.

a11y.describedBy: aria-describedby is written on opening and removed on closing: pointing at an id that is no longer in the document is an invalid value, and an invalid attribute is worse than a missing one.
a11y.duplicateName: The duplicated name. If the text equals the control's accessible name, the panel goes aria-hidden: the aria-label already says the name, and connecting it through aria-describedby would announce it twice. If it adds information, it is connected and takes role="tooltip". The directive does not guess: whoever uses it declares it, with describes.
a11y.escape: Escape is listened for on the document, not on the host: a tooltip opened by hover has the focus somewhere else, and a local listener would never see the key there.
a11y.hoverAndFocus: It appears on hover AND on keyboard focus. Hover only would leave keyboard users out, and the icon-only button would be useless to them. It listens for focusin/focusout —the ones that bubble— so it also works on a container whose focusable element is a descendant.

anatomy.caption: Tokens that [ewmsTooltip] consumes
anatomy.intro:
The panel is a hand-built
with a single class string: it has no Angular template, so everything that paints it is in that string and comes from these tokens.
anatomy.textContent: The text is written with textContent, never innerHTML: a tooltip cannot carry markup, whether by accident or through a value that comes from data.

contract.inputs: The four in the table in block 3. Two ways to write them, and the name changes on purpose: inside a system component the input is simply called tooltip, because the component's selector already carries the prefix; on any other element the directive uses [ewmsTooltip], because a bare [tooltip] is a global attribute selector too generic, and it would clash with any other library.
contract.outputs: None. The directive opens and closes its own panel; there is nothing the consumer needs to know.

demo.describes: The descriptive one. The text ADDS information the name does not give, so it is connected with aria-describedby and announced as a description. On an arbitrary element the selector is prefixed: [ewmsTooltip].
demo.duplicate: The repeated name. label and tooltip say the same thing, so the panel goes aria-hidden and the screen reader announces it only once. Give it focus with Tab: it appears all the same.
demo.exportHint: Exports the 1,482 visible rows, not the whole table
demo.frame: The directive on three different hosts
demo.suppressedStatus: tooltipDisabled = {{ value }}. What goes off is the description; the button's name —its own text— stays. A switch that could leave a control without a name would not be a tooltip switch.

header.directive: It is a directive, not a component

mistakes.disabled: Assuming there is a disabled. There is not, and the name of what does exist —tooltipDisabled— is structural. This directive goes on controls, and disabled is a property of every native control: an input with that name swallows the [disabled] of its own host. Angular binds it to the directive, the native attribute is never written, and the result is a button that looks disabled and can still be clicked. It fails silently, on exactly the attribute where failing silently is worst.
mistakes.foundBy: Believing a review found it. It was found by two icon-only button tests that failed. The first way out was writing [attr.disabled] in the consumer, but that leaves the trap alive for every system component that puts a tooltip on a native control. Renaming the input closes it at the root. There is a regression test, and it was checked that it bites: reintroducing the clash makes the test fail.
mistakes.inputName: Writing ewmsTooltip as the input name inside a system component. There it is called tooltip. The prefix belongs to the directive's selector, for when it is applied to an arbitrary element.
mistakes.interactive: Putting a link or a button inside. There is no way to reach it with the keyboard: the focus is on the host and the panel is not focusable.
mistakes.touch: Expecting it to appear on a tablet. Today it does not: there is no hover or focus to trigger it. That is acceptable because it is never the only source of the information — and that “because” is what must be preserved.

tooltip.notApplicable: Two, written above rather than deleted: state matrix (only one tooltip can be open per page) and sizes (the panel fits its text).

props.caption: Inputs of the [ewmsTooltip] directive
props.describes: Whether the text ADDS information to the accessible name. false connects nothing and makes the panel aria-hidden; true connects it with aria-describedby and role="tooltip". The directive does not guess: whoever uses it declares it.
props.position: Preferred placement. It flips to the opposite side by itself when it does not fit: the list the CDK walks has two entries, the requested one and its opposite.
props.text: Required. The text, already translated by the consumer. It is the selector AND the input: applying the directive and giving it its text are the same attribute. Inside a DS component it is exposed simply as tooltip.
props.tooltipDisabled: Suppresses the tooltip in a specific context without removing the directive. It is NOT called disabled, and the prefix is structural: see Common mistakes.

purpose.notAHint: It does not replace a field's help. That is the Input's hint, which is always visible.
purpose.notAName: It is not the accessible name of anything. A tooltip describes; it does not name. Keyboard users may never see it and on a touch screen there is no hover: a control whose only name is its tooltip has no name.
purpose.notLongText: It is not a container for long text, let alone interactive content: a link or a button inside cannot be reached with the keyboard.
purpose.scope: It entered the system because the icon-only button requires it. The scope is deliberate: the minimum that consumer needs, done well.
purpose.solves: Short text that appears next to a control when you point at it or focus it. It goes on an element that already exists: it wraps nothing, has no template, and the panel is built as a DOM node inside a CDK overlay.

rules.caption: Content on hover or focus — a requirement, not an enhancement

columns.check: How to check it on this page

dismissible.check: Open any of the ones above and press Escape: it disappears and the focus stays where it was.
dismissible.means: Escape closes it without moving the focus or the pointer.
dismissible.name: Dismissible

hoverable.check: Point at a control, move slowly to the panel and stay there: it does not go away.
hoverable.means: The pointer can move into the panel without it closing.
hoverable.name: Hoverable

rules.keyboard: On keyboard focus there is no delay: moving with Tab is deliberate, nobody passes a control by accident.

persistent.check: Leave it open and wait. It is still there.
persistent.means: It stays visible until the pointer leaves, the focus moves away or Escape is pressed. It never closes on a timer.
persistent.name: Persistent

rules.timers: There are two timers and neither of them closes it automatically. One is the delay before it appears, which exists so that sweeping the mouse across a toolbar does not fire five tooltips on the way. The other is the margin the pointer has to travel from the control to the panel —what the “hoverable” rule requires—, and entering the panel cancels it.
rules.title: The three WCAG 2.2 §1.4.13 rules, and how to test them here

sizes.fits: There is no Small/Medium/Large scale: the panel fits its text, with a maximum width so that a long sentence wraps onto several lines instead of crossing the screen.
sizes.limit: That cap is also the reminder of what this component is not: if the text does not fit comfortably, it was not a tooltip.

states.behaviour: A grid of “open” cells would therefore be a grid where every cell but one is lying. What can truly be rendered is the behaviour, and that is the table below.
states.oneOpen: A tooltip has two states, closed and open, and only one can be open on the whole page: opening one closes the previous one, through a module-level registry that the buttons of a toolbar share without knowing about each other.
states.title: Does not apply — and the reason is interesting

bottom.hint: Below; moves up if it does not fit.
bottom.label: bottom

variants.intro: There are no style variants: there are four placements. Each declares the preferred one, and the CDK walks a list of two —the requested one and its opposite— keeping the first that fits. That is the automatic flip, and it is not decoration: a tooltip cut off by the edge of the window is a useless tooltip.

left.hint: To the left; moves to the right if it does not fit.
left.label: left

variants.noGap: There is no gap between the control and the panel. A gap would be dead space the pointer has to cross, and 1.4.13 requires the tooltip to stay open while the pointer travels towards it.

right.hint: To the right; moves to the left if it does not fit.
right.label: right

top.hint: Above; drops below if it does not fit.
top.label: top (default)

families.mono: The mono family is still the system stack: JetBrains Mono comes in with its first real consumer, the Table. Until then the token exists and points to the stack, which is the honest thing to do — you do not declare a face that is not being served.
families.title: The two families

gaps.body: Four values are still undecided in tokens.css: the line height of H4, that of Caption, and the weight and line height of Mono. Above, they are marked (pending) instead of being filled in with an invented number or having their row deleted. In the meantime the browser applies its normal value, which is exactly what you are seeing.
gaps.title: The gaps are information, not neglect

header.intro: A single interface family: Montserrat, variable 100–900, self-hosted. It is not loaded from a CDN — the CSP only allows font-src 'self'. The mono family plays a supporting role, for codes and SKUs.

rule.coupled: The visual level and the semantic level are coupled, and there is no as prop, nor a level one, to separate them.

caption.use: Metadata and timestamps. It takes the secondary colour.

h3.use: Subsection, or the heading of a card.

h4.use: Highlighted label. The capitals are applied by the component, not by the text.

p.sample: The operator confirms the quantity received before closing the receipt.

weights.fromScale: All four come from the scale tokens, not from the weight primitives: gate 10 rejects a primitive outside tokens.css, and besides, the weight that matters here is “the one the body uses”, not “400”.
weights.medium: Medium, the weight of the controls
weights.range: If all four looked the same and thin, the font-weight: 100 900 in the @font-face has been lost: without the range the browser treats the face as a single weight and renders everything at the axis default, which is Thin.
